A parallel scan hands out level-1 downlinks, so it cannot turn a
"col = ANY (array)" qualification into one descent per element the way
the serial scan does (switch_to_next_range()).  Its key range is the
union [smallest element, largest element], and every leaf in between is

array that is nearly the whole index, and the planner does not see it:

parallel plan that loses to the serial one.

callback -- it is consulted before both the in-memory and the on-disk
branch -- and only the level-1 internal chain, a small fraction of the
tree, is still walked in full.

interleaved with every value

Let the checkpointer wait for lock table room

o_tables_rel_lock_extended() already retries the per-tree lock when the
checkpointer cannot take it right away, because the holder may be blocked
in RegisterSyncRequest() waiting for the checkpointer to drain the sync
queue.  But LockAcquire() does not only fail to acquire; it also raises
"out of shared memory" when the lock table has no room left, and that
error escapes the loop.

That is what took the checkpointer down in issue #1053: a fuzzer's worth
of concurrent DDL had filled the table, and the checkpoint died on the
first user tree it tried to lock.  The previous commit turns such an
error into an exit rather than a retry of a half-rotated checkpoint, but
this one need not be an error at all -- the table is full of other
backends' locks, and it empties again as they finish.  So ask for
LOCKACQUIRE_NOT_AVAIL in that case too and let the existing loop come
back for it.

Keep FETCH-mode locators on the page image, and stop lying about partial reads

Two related defects in the FETCH (partial page image) read path.

partial_load_chunk() returned early whenever the chunk was already in the
image, without positioning the caller's locator.  But callers pass a
locator precisely to have it positioned on that chunk, so it was left
wherever it happened to be -- on another chunk, or, when
fastpath_find_downlink() produced it, pointing into the live shared page
rather than the image.  Reading a tuple through the latter bypasses the
copy-then-validate protocol entirely, so the bytes can be torn.  Fall
through for an already-loaded chunk whenever a locator is supplied, and
skip only the memcpy.

find_page() then converts a fastpath-produced locator onto the image
before storing it, so nothing downstream can follow a locator into the
source page.

page and only looks at the locator's own cache

pg_upgrade: evaluate index-expression SQL functions via o_fmgr_sql in recovery

Index expressions/predicates are compiled with ExecInitExpr/ExecInitQual, which
give a SQL function PostgreSQL's native fmgr_sql -- it parses AND executes the
body against the catalog.  In a catalog-free context (recovery, checkpointer)
there is no catalog, so replaying an insert into such an index segfaults in the
SQL-function executor (postquel_sub_params via o_get_idx_expr_att -> fmgr_sql).

After compiling, redirect SQL-function calls (fn_addr == fmgr_sql) to o_fmgr_sql,
which evaluates from the parse trees cached in the OrioleDB proc cache -- the
same fixup already done for opclass comparators in descr.c.  ExecInterpExpr
calls the cached step->d.func.fn_addr copy directly (the finfo indirection is
bypassed for speed), so that copy must be redirected too.  Gated on
o_is_syscache_hooks_set(), so foreground execution keeps native fmgr_sql against
the real catalog.

ring_buffer: fix off-by-one in wrapped iov regions

The two "wrapped" cases in ring_buffer_get_read_iov and
ring_buffer_get_write_iov subtracted one byte too many, treating the
reserved sentinel byte as if it always sat at the physical end of the
buffer.

In ring_buffer_get_read_iov the sentinel lives in the free region
[tail, head), not in [head, size), so the trailing read region must not
be shortened.  In ring_buffer_get_write_iov the byte before head is only
at the buffer end when head == 0.

The result was that pty output could be truncated/garbled once the ring
buffer wrapped and was drained partially.

Add two regression tests: a deterministic replay of the reported
scenario and a randomized stress test that verifies byte-exact FIFO
ordering across wraps for a range of capacities.

ring_buffer: fix off-by-one in wrapped iov regions

The two "wrapped" cases in ring_buffer_get_read_iov and
ring_buffer_get_write_iov subtracted one byte too many, treating the
reserved sentinel byte as if it always sat at the physical end of the
buffer.

In ring_buffer_get_read_iov the sentinel lives in the free region
[tail, head), not in [head, size), so the trailing read region must not
be shortened.  In ring_buffer_get_write_iov the byte before head is only
at the buffer end when head == 0.

The result was that pty output could be truncated/garbled once the ring
buffer wrapped and was drained partially.

Add two regression tests: a deterministic replay of the reported
scenario and a randomized stress test that verifies byte-exact FIFO
ordering across wraps for a range of capacities.

Fixes: https://github.com/containers/crun/issues/2207

segment: Permission denied" (#2176).

mountpoi

check_fd_under_path() requires a '/' right after the rootfs prefix, so

column6:
chroot_realpath: keep separator when expanding a relative symlink

When the last resolved component is a relative symlink, the code backs
up over it with

	while (*(--new_path) != '/');

leaving new_path pointing at the separator itself, so the expanded
symlink target overwrites it.  "<root>/dir/link" with "link" pointing to
"file" resolves to "<root>/dirfile" instead of "<root>/dir/file", and
"<root>/link" resolves to "<root>link".

Top level symlinks happen to survive since safe_openat_fallback() strips
the rootfs prefix and then consumes leading slashes, but any relative
symlink below the first level resolves to a path that does not exist,
and the open fails with ENOENT.

Keep the separator after backing up over the component.  This is only
reachable through the safe_openat() fallback, i.e. on kernels without
openat2(2) or when a seccomp filter blocks it.

Add unit tests for symlink expansion, which was not covered at all.

linux: add OPEN_TREE_NAMESPACE support

Use open_tree(OPEN_TREE_NAMESPACE) + setns(CLONE_NEWNS) to replace the
traditional unshare(CLONE_NEWNS) + bind mount rootfs + pivot_root
sequence.

OPEN_TREE_NAMESPACE creates a new mount namespace with the rootfs as
the root mount.  setns() enters that namespace directly, so no bind
mount or pivot_root is needed.  The kernel automatically sets the
process root and cwd to the new namespace's root when the old root is
not reachable.

On older kernels (< 7.0) or when OPEN_TREE_NAMESPACE is not
supported, the code falls back to the traditional path.

Closes: https://github.com/containers/crun/issues/2086

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.6 <noreply@anthropic.com>

ioexpander/ch422g: add a driver for the WCH CH422G I/O

The CH422G offers eight bi-directional pins, IO0-IO7, and four open-drain
outputs, OC0-OC3.  It appears on boards that have run out of usable GPIOs
once a parallel RGB panel has taken its share, the Waveshare
ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-7 among them, where it holds the panel and touch
controller in and out of reset and switches the backlight.

Two things about the device do not fit the shape a register-per-address
I2C driver usually takes, and both are handled here rather than pushed on
to board logic:

  - A register is selected by the I2C address the transfer is addressed
    to, not by a register address written ahead of the data.  Each access
    carries a single byte to one of four addresses.
  - None of the write-only registers can be read back, so the driver
    keeps a shadow copy of each and updates it in step with the device.

IO0-IO7 have no individual direction control; one bit of the system
parameter register drives the whole

boards/nucleo-l073rz: Add USB device support and a CDC/ACM configuration.

The STM32L073RZ provides a full speed USB device controller, but the
Nucleo-L073RZ board support did not enable it and no configuration
exercised it.

Add the pieces required to run USB device mode on this board:

- Add the USB device pin definitions to the STM32L0 pin map.
- Provide board level pull-up control using the embedded DP pull-up in
  USB_BCDR, and register the CDC/ACM class at boot when it is selected.
- Add a usb-cdc configuration that presents an NSH console on USART2 and
  a CDC/ACM serial device on USB.

The 48MHz clock for the controller is supplied by HSI48 trimmed from the
USB start of frame packet, which is the crystal-less USB configuration
already described by this board's board.h.

Add period-aware octave transposition for tuned scales, closes #8137 (#8338)

* Add period-aware octave transposition for tuned scales, closes #8137

When "Transpose Octave by Tuning Period" is enabled (off by default),
the oscillator and scene octave parameters shift by one period of the
current tuning rather than a fixed 12 semitones.

Behaviour by mode when the option is on:
  RETUNE_ALL        — octaveSize = scale.count (e.g. 13 for Bohlen-Pierce,
                      19 for ED2-19); same result as the prior implicit
                      behaviour, now made explicit and toggleable.
  RETUNE_MIDI_ONLY  — octaveSize = last-tone cents / 100, so a BP scale
                      shifts by ~19.02 semitones (the 3:1 tritave) rather
                      than the usual 12-semitone octave.
  MTS               — octaveSize = MTS_GetPeriodSemitones().

When the option is off the prior behaviour is preserved exactly:
  RETUNE_ALL + non-standard tuning → scale.count; everything else → 12.

cgroup: check buffer bounds when constructing cgroup paths

`prepare_cgroup_dir_properties()` and `prepare_cgroup_dirs()` append
nested cgroup directory names to a fixed-size path buffer with
`sprintf()`, without checking the remaining space. A sufficiently deep
or long cgroup hierarchy can write past the end of the buffer. To fix
this, introduce a helper, `append_cgroup_dir()`, that uses `snprintf()`
and verifies the result fits in the buffer, and pass the buffer size
down through the recursive calls. Restore now fails with an error
message when a cgroup path does not fit.

As a global variable with the name `n_controllers` already exists, we
use `n_cnames` instead.

Add a ZDTM test that verifies inotify watches on files inside an
overlayfs mount survive checkpoint/restore.

The test uses the external mount pattern (like mnt_ext_auto): in
the ZDTM_NEWNS=1 phase it creates an overlay mount before

does not attempt to reconstruct the overlay on restore.  After

inotify watch itself is properly dumped and restored by exercising

setup requires the ZDTM_NEWNS=1 lifecycle and root privileges
for mounting overlayfs.

zdtm: add cow02 to cover a PROT_NONE COW root

Add a test for the SIGSEGV fixed by "mem: keep COW root VMAs writable
when premapping".

The parent reserves an address range with PROT_NONE and never touches
it, so the kernel does not account it (no "ac" flag in smaps). After
fork(), the child turns the same range into a writable mapping and fills
it with data. CRIU matches COW VMAs by start/end and flags but ignores
their protection bits, so the parent's PROT_NONE, not-accountable VMA
becomes the COW root of the child's data VMA.

On restore the child inherits the root's mapping. Without the fix that
mapping is PROT_NONE, so restoring the child's pages into it faults and
the test fails at restore; with the fix it passes.

test: add multishot accept stress test

Add accept-mshot-stress to stress test multishot accept under rapid
connection churn. Three sub-tests:

- test_accept_mshot_stress: a client thread makes 200 rapid
  connect+close cycles while the server uses multishot accept,
  re-arming when F_MORE drops. Verifies all connections accepted.
- test_accept_mshot_burst: client opens 32 connections at once
  (held open), server drains all accepts, client closes. Repeats
  for 4 rounds with barrier synchronization between phases.
- test_accept_mshot_reconnect: client connects, sends 1 byte,
  closes, and reconnects 100 times. Server accepts each connection
  and reads the byte to verify end-to-end data delivery through
  the accept+recv path.

test: add per-task io_uring restrictions test

Add task-restrict to test per-task io_uring restrictions, which are
registered via io_uring_register(fd=-1, IORING_REGISTER_RESTRICTIONS)
and apply to all rings subsequently created by that task. Four
sub-tests, each running in a forked child since task restrictions
cannot be removed once set:

- test_task_restrict_sqe_op: registers a restriction allowing only
  NOP, then verifies NOP succeeds while read is denied with -EACCES.
- test_task_restrict_fork_inherit: registers restrictions in a child,
  forks a grandchild, and verifies the grandchild's rings inherit
  the same restrictions.
- test_task_restrict_double_register: verifies that registering task
  restrictions a second time fails with -EPERM.
- test_task_restrict_register_op: restricts register operations to
  only IORING_REGISTER_FILES, verifying that register_buffers is
  denied with -EACCES.

Each child calls prctl(PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS) before registering, as
the kernel requires

test: add multishot recv buffer exhaustion stress test

Add recv-mshot-drain to stress test multishot recv when the buffer
ring runs dry during active receives. Uses an intentionally small
buffer ring (4 buffers) while a sender thread pushes 32 messages,
forcing repeated buffer exhaustion.

The test handles both exhaustion signals: -ENOBUFS CQEs and the
absence of IORING_CQE_F_MORE on completions. In both cases it
refills the buffer ring and re-arms the multishot recv. Verifies
that all sent data is received correctly after the full sequence
of drain/refill cycles.

test: add NOP flags test

Add nop-flags to test the NOP operation flags that allow exercising
kernel code paths without real I/O:

- IORING_NOP_INJECT_RESULT: inject a specific result value (also
  used to detect NOP flags support).
- IORING_NOP_FILE: perform a normal fd lookup, verified with both
  valid and invalid fds.
- IORING_NOP_FIXED_FILE: perform a fixed file table lookup.
- IORING_NOP_FIXED_BUFFER: perform a registered buffer lookup,
  verified with both valid and invalid buffer indices.
- IORING_NOP_TW: complete via the task_work path instead of
  inline completion.
- IORING_NOP_CQE32: pass extra1/extra2 values through big CQEs,
  including verification that it requires a CQE32/CQE_MIXED ring.
- Combined test exercising all flags together.

Each sub-feature is detected independently so the test gracefully
skips on kernels that don't support specific flags.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.6 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Jens Axboe <axboe@kernel.dk>

Add cancel-race to stress test the race between cancellation and
completion of io_uring operations. Three sub-tests:

The prompt appeared, and then both the prompt and Task Explorer vanished with no
elevated instance to show for it.

pkexec names its *parent* as the polkit subject, so exiting while the prompt is
still on screen invalidates the request: polkit drops it, pkexec never execs
anything, and the dialog disappears. The old code waited a flat 2.5 seconds,

concluded success and closed. Anyone slower than two and a half seconds at typing
a password therefore lost both windows. My "the lesser problem of the two" comment
was simply wrong: it is the worse one.

pkexec reported:

    Refusing to render service to dead parents.

It checks getppid() at startup and refuses if it has been orphaned, and
QProcess::startDetached deliberately double-forks so that what it starts is
reparented away from the caller. So pkexec was orphaned before it ever ran.

This is why it failed on a Raspberry Pi but not on a desktop: a session with a
user-level systemd has a subreaper, so the orphan is adopted by that rather than
by pid 1 and pkexec tolerates it. Measured here - the double-forked child was
adopted by systemd --user at pid 959, not by init. Without a subreaper it lands on

Never start the privileged helper from a GUI-thread getter

Selecting a process froze the UI. The process panel fills in its fields from
const getters on the GUI thread, and two of them reached for TaskHelper without
checking the opt-in setting:

    ProcessView.cpp:466   m_pCurDir->setText(pProcess->GetWorkingDirectory())
    EnvironmentView.cpp   pProcess->GetEnvVariables()

Neither /proc/<pid>/cwd nor /proc/<pid>/environ is readable for another user's
process, so for anything root-owned the direct read returned empty and the getter
called RunWorker(true) - which launches pkexec and then waits for the socket to
appear for up to 60 seconds, because an elevated start has an authentication
prompt in the middle of it. On the GUI thread that is indistinguishable from the
application having hung, and it repeated on every click. Most visible running as
an ordinary user, where most processes belong to someone else, which is why it
showed up on a Raspberry Pi and not on a desktop run as root.

The aarch64 build failed with

far better than refusing to build.

field order (uc_flags, uc_link, uc_stack, uc_mcontext, uc_sigmask), and that is
not the order everywhere: on aarch64 glibc puts uc_sigmask *before* uc_mcontext.

TaskExplorer was Windows-only. This adds a Linux port alongside it, driven by
the same CMake description intended to build both.

Build
- Replace the qmake .pro/.pri files with CMake. The .vcxproj files remain as
  the reference for what the Windows build contained. The Windows build has
  not been compiled from CMake yet.

Linux backend (TaskExplorer/API/Linux)
- Processes, threads, handles, modules, memory maps and windows from /proc,
  sock_diag netlink for sockets, systemd over D-Bus for daemons, /proc/modules
  and /sys/module for drivers.
- Views with no Windows counterpart: control groups, LSM/seccomp security,
  pressure stall information.
- ELF core dumps in the same format the kernel and gcore produce, verified
  loadable in gdb with full backtraces.
- X11 window enumeration, including processes that set no _NET_WM_PID, via the
  X-Resource extension.

Add Linux support: CMake build, /proc backend, privileged helper, bundling

TaskExplorer was Windows-only. This adds a Linux port alongside it, driven by
the same CMake description intended to build both.

Build
- Replace the qmake .pro/.pri files with CMake. The .vcxproj files remain as
  the reference for what the Windows build contained. The Windows build has
  not been compiled from CMake yet.

Linux backend (TaskExplorer/API/Linux)
- Processes, threads, handles, modules, memory maps and windows from /proc,
  sock_diag netlink for sockets, systemd over D-Bus for daemons, /proc/modules
  and /sys/module for drivers.
- Views with no Windows counterpart: control groups, LSM/seccomp security,
  pressure stall information.
- ELF core dumps in the same format the kernel and gcore produce, verified
  loadable in gdb with full backtraces.
- X11 window enumeration, including processes that set no _NET_WM_PID, via the
  X-Resource extension.

- Views with no Windows counterpart: control groups, LSM/seccomp security,
  pressure stall information.
- ELF core dumps in the same format the kernel and gcore produce, verified
  loadable in gdb with full backtraces.
- X11 window enumeration, including processes that set no _NET_WM_PID, via the
  X-Resource extension.

Add Linux support: CMake build, /proc backend, privileged helper, bundling

TaskExplorer was Windows-only. This adds a Linux port alongside it, driven by
the same CMake description intended to build both.

Build
- Replace the qmake .pro/.pri files with CMake. The .vcxproj files remain as
  the reference for what the Windows build contained. The Windows build has
  not been compiled from CMake yet.

Linux backend (TaskExplorer/API/Linux)
- Processes, threads, handles, modules, memory maps and windows from /proc,
  sock_diag netlink for sockets, systemd over D-Bus for daemons, /proc/modules
  and /sys/module for drivers.
- Views with no Windows counterpart: control groups, LSM/seccomp security,
  pressure stall information.
- ELF core dumps in the same format the kernel and gcore produce, verified
  loadable in gdb with full backtraces.
- X11 window enumeration, including processes that set no _NET_WM_PID, via the
  X-Resource extension.

Add Linux support: CMake build, /proc backend, privileged helper, bundling

TaskExplorer was Windows-only. This adds a Linux port alongside it, driven by
the same CMake description intended to build both.

Build
- Replace the qmake .pro/.pri files with CMake. The .vcxproj files remain as
  the reference for what the Windows build contained. The Windows build has
  not been compiled from CMake yet.

Linux backend (TaskExplorer/API/Linux)
- Processes, threads, handles, modules, memory maps and windows from /proc,
  sock_diag netlink for sockets, systemd over D-Bus for daemons, /proc/modules
  and /sys/module for drivers.
- Views with no Windows counterpart: control groups, LSM/seccomp security,
  pressure stall information.
- ELF core dumps in the same format the kernel and gcore produce, verified
  loadable in gdb with full backtraces.
- X11 window enumeration, including processes that set no _NET_WM_PID, via the
  X-Resource extension.

static quint32 TcpStateToMib(quint32 LinuxState)
{
	switch (LinuxState)
	{
		case 1:  return 5;	// TCP_ESTABLISHED -> MIB_TCP_STATE_ESTAB
		case 2:  return 3;	// TCP_SYN_SENT    -> MIB_TCP_STATE_SYN_SENT
		case 3:  return 4;	// TCP_SYN_RECV    -> MIB_TCP_STATE_SYN_RCVD
		case 4:  return 6;	// TCP_FIN_WAIT1   -> MIB_TCP_STATE_FIN_WAIT1
		case 5:  return 7;	// TCP_FIN_WAIT2   -> MIB_TCP_STATE_FIN_WAIT2
		case 6:  return 11;	// TCP_TIME_WAIT   -> MIB_TCP_STATE_TIME_WAIT
		case 7:  return 1;	// TCP_CLOSE       -> MIB_TCP_STATE_CLOSED
		case 8:  return 8;	// TCP_CLOSE_WAIT  -> MIB_TCP_STATE_CLOSE_WAIT
		case 9:  return 10;	// TCP_LAST_ACK    -> MIB_TCP_STATE_LAST_ACK
		case 10: return 2;	// TCP_LISTEN      -> MIB_TCP_STATE_LISTEN
		case 11: return 9;	// TCP_CLOSING     -> MIB_TCP_STATE_CLOSING
	}
	return 0;
}

Return the class name atom from JS_GetClassName() (#1641)

* Return the class name atom from JS_GetClassName()

JS_GetClassName() duplicates and returns rt->class_array[class_id].class_id,
the numeric JSClassID, where a JSAtom is expected. The two fields are
adjacent in JSClass and both 32-bit, so the mistake compiles cleanly, but
the value handed to JS_DupAtomRT() is a class id reinterpreted as an atom:
for a class id below JS_ATOM_END it bumps the refcount of an unrelated
predefined atom and returns it, and above that it indexes into the runtime
atom array out of any relation to the class.

Return .class_name instead.

[lib][libcpp] add <atomic> over the compiler's __atomic builtins

std::atomic<T> for integral, enum, and pointer types, with the full
load/store/exchange/compare_exchange/fetch_* surface, the operator
sugar, memory_order, thread/signal fences, atomic_flag, and the
standard typedefs. Pointer arithmetic scales by element size.

The load-bearing policy is a static_assert on __atomic_always_lock_free:
no instantiation can generate a libatomic call, so atomic<uint64_t> on
riscv32/armv7 is a readable compile-time error instead of a link
failure. The generic (address-based) builtin forms are used for
load/store/exchange/CAS because clang restricts the _n forms to
integer/pointer types, rejecting enums.

Deviations: no atomic<struct>/atomic<float>, no C++20 wait/notify, no
volatile overloads.

Tests include an SMP smoke test (two threads hammering fetch_add) plus
semantic checks of every operation; run on arm64 and riscv32.

The commonly used non-allocating algorithms, iterator-pair based:
min/max/minmax/clamp (with comparator and initializer_list forms),

indexing algorithms assume random access iterators. Query algorithms
are constexpr ahead of C++20.

[kernel][test] make the port group tests robust to failure paths

Same treatment as two_threads_race and group_basic: a failed ASSERT in
group_dynamic or group_waiting returned straight out of the test,
leaking the named test ports and poisoning every later run of the case
with ERR_ALREADY_EXISTS. Move the fallible middle of each test into a
body function that records what it has created, and have the caller run
an unconditional cleanup that joins the receiver and releases whatever
the body left behind.

While at it, make make_port_pair tear down the write side if opening
the read side fails, and have receive_thread report any read error
rather than only a timeout.

[kernel][test] drive the port test worker threads to exit on failure paths

In two_threads_race and group_basic a failed ASSERT between spawning the
worker threads and joining them returned straight out of the test,
leaving the workers blocked forever on their ports and the named ports
alive, which turned any single failure into a permanent
ERR_ALREADY_EXISTS failure of the whole case for the rest of the boot.

Move the fallible middle of each test into a body function that records
what it has opened, and have the caller run an unconditional shutdown
path that signals the starting line, tells the workers to quit, joins
them and releases whatever the body left behind. Also bound every wait
on a worker thread so one dying unexpectedly fails the test instead of
hanging the boot until the CI timeout.

[app][shell][lib][unittest] run a script from the kernel command line at boot

Add an lk.autorun kernel command line variable holding a shell script, which the
shell app runs through the console before dropping into the interactive loop.
Spaces may be written as '+' ('++' for a literal plus) so a script survives the
layers of host side scripting and command line handling without being quoted; a
quoted value works too, since lib/cmdline already unquotes it.

This is meant to be the general way to drive a target from a host script:
start qemu and tell it what to run, rather than adding a command line variable
per scenario. Drop the first of those, lk.unittests_at_boot, which hardcoded a
"sleep 5; ut all" script, and have run-qemu-boot-tests.py ask for that script
directly instead. It now ends the script with poweroff so qemu exits on its own,
which in turn means the harness has to drain the pipe to real EOF rather than
stopping as soon as the process is reaped.

[arch][test] move the float context switch test to arch/test

The floating point test checks that FPU register state survives context
switching, which is architecture support code, so move it next to the mmu
tests and convert it to lib/unittest. It already compared against exact
reference values but only printed the mismatch, so it could not fail.

Two things had to change to make it pass portably, both found by running it
on every architecture for the first time:

- compare with a relative tolerance instead of exact bit patterns. x87 on 32
  bit x86 and the 68881/68040 on m68k compute in 80 bit extended precision,
  so the low bits legitimately drift over a million iterations. The observed
  drift is about 1e-14 relative; the tolerance is 1e-9.
- build with -ffp-contract=off and regenerate the reference values. The old
  table was captured from a build that contracted the multiply-adds into fma,
  which is 1 ulp away from the uncontracted result and varies by compiler and
  architectu

[kernel][test] convert the self validating thread tests to unit tests

The mutex, semaphore, event, atomic and join tests in app/tests were already
checking real invariants, but only printed their verdict, so a regression
looked identical to a pass. Move them to kernel/test as lib/unittest cases so
they run under `ut all` and fail the boot tests when they break.

Beyond the mechanical EXPECT_*/ASSERT_* conversion:

- shrink the workloads to fit the 30 second per architecture boot test
  budget: the mutex test drops from 1000000 to 1000 iterations per thread,
  the atomic test from 10000000 to 10000, the semaphore test from 10000 to
  2000 waits, and the mutex timeout drops from 1s to 100ms.
- the event tests previously proved nothing: they slept two seconds and
  destroyed the event without ever checking who woke up. They now count
  wakeups and assert that a plain event wakes every waiter while an
  EVENT_FLAG_AUTOUNSIGNAL event wakes exactly one.
- the join test read t->magic after t

[lib][fs][fat][test] add malformed BPB mount tests

Corrupt one field of a freshly formatted volume at a time and check that mount
rejects it rather than trusting it: total sectors larger than the device in both
the 16 and 32 bit fields, zero and non-power-of-two and absurd sectors per
cluster, an unsupported sector size, zero and absurd FAT counts, a bad media
descriptor, a root entry count that is not a whole number of sectors, and a zero
sectors per FAT.

These are cheap on a RAM disk and impossible to build with mkfs.fat, which is
why the driver's input validation had never been exercised. The volume is
restored and remounted afterwards, so a rejected mount is also shown to leave
nothing behind.

[lib][fs][fat][test] add a stress suite

Six tests that are deliberately slower and more destructive than the
correctness ones, gated behind test.fat.stress=1 so the default boot-time
`ut all` path stays fast. scripts/run-fat-tests.py --stress sets the flag and
raises the QEMU timeout to match. They run against RAM backed volumes, so no
disk image is needed and they work on any architecture.

  remount        write a couple of dozen files, then round trip through the
                 device three times verifying every byte. Nothing covered this
                 before, which is how the directory entry offset bug survived:
                 the old tests only ever read a size back from memory.

  enospc         fill the volume until writes fail, check the failure is a sane
                 error rather than a corrupted success, check every file written
                 before it is still intact, remount, then free everything and
                 confirm the free space comes back exactly.

[lib][fs][fat][test] replace the FAT test shell scripts with data driven python

mkblk was twenty unrolled mcopy lines under set -x that had to be cd'd into,
took no arguments and rebuilt everything every time, including a 4GB FAT32
image. run-fat-tests.sh was hardcoded to arm64 and validated the result with
fsck.fat alone, which checks the metadata graph but says nothing about whether
the bytes the guest wrote are the bytes it meant to write.

mkimage.py builds the images from a table of geometries and a content manifest,
skips images that are already up to date, and emits a JSON manifest of what
each image should contain. Generated payloads now carry a position dependent
pattern instead of being dd'd from /dev/zero: a misplaced cluster usually reads
back as zeroes, so a zero filled file cannot detect one.

It also checks that each image really is the FAT width it asked for. mkfs.fat
honours -F even when the cluster count is out of range for that width, and it

[lib][fs][fat][test] add self-contained RAM backed FAT tests

These format a volume in a heap buffer with fs_format_device() and need no disk
image, no kernel command line and no host tooling, so they run on every
architecture in CI. That is what stops the FAT tests from passing vacuously when
no disk is attached, which is what happens today: 13 of the 18 existing tests
skip and report as passed.

ram_volume is an RAII wrapper over memalign + create_membdev + format + mount,
with a remount() helper. create() returns ERR_NO_MEMORY when the buffer will not
fit so a test can skip a geometry that is too large for the target instead of
failing on it; the sweep reports how many ran and fails if none did.

A FAT driver is really three drivers, and which one you get is decided by the
cluster count alone, so the sweep pins each geometry to an exact count by
solving for the volume size rather than estimating it:

  fat12-min             64 clusters
  fat12-max           4084 clusters   last FAT1

[lib][fs][fat][test] make a skipped device test visible and optionally fatal

SKIP_TEST_IF_NO_DEVICE() returns true when test.fat.device is unset, so the 13
device-backed FAT tests report as passed without touching a filesystem. CI runs
run-qemu-boot-tests.py with no disk attached, so that is exactly what happens

[lib][fs][fat] implement the fs_stat hook

The fat_api vtable left .fs_stat null, so 'fs stat' on a FAT mount returned
ERR_NOT_SUPPORTED and tests had no way to query the mounted volume's geometry
at runtime.

Report total space as the data cluster count times the cluster size. For free
space, prefer a valid FAT32 FSInfo free count and otherwise walk the active FAT
counting zero entries via fat_next_cluster_in_chain(), which already handles all
three FAT widths including the FAT12 entry that straddles a sector boundary.

FAT has no inode table, so both inode counts are reported as zero.

Verified against a 16MB FAT16 image: both this and mtools' mdir report
16115712 bytes free.

nvmf: deduplicate tgt/subsystem lookup with _rpc_nvmf_get_subsystem

Many NVMe-oF RPC handlers repeat the same spdk_nvmf_get_tgt() +
spdk_nvmf_tgt_find_subsystem() sequence with identical error
handling.  Extract this into a static helper that returns the
subsystem or NULL after sending the appropriate JSON-RPC error
response.

An optional tgt_out parameter lets callers that need the
intermediate tgt pointer (e.g. for ctx->tgt) reuse the helper
instead of open-coding the lookup.

The nqn parameter is optional: when NULL the helper performs only
the target lookup, populates tgt_out, and returns NULL without
error.  This lets rpc_nvmf_get_subsystems use the same helper for
its tgt-only path (NVMF_SUBSYSTEM_FOREACH) while the subsystem
lookup is enforced by the decoder in every other caller.

Error responses now distinguish user faults from system errors:
  - explicit tgt_name not found  -> INVALID_PARAMS
  - no default target resolved   -> INTERNAL_ERROR
  - subsystem NQN not found

`bool visible` dispatch are eliminated — each paused callback calls
spdk_nvmf_ns_add_host() or spdk_nvmf_ns_remove_host() directly.

* tests/util: Make native_module_helper_t safely movable

native_module_helper_t owns a generated .sys file that the destructor
deletes when _delete_file_on_destruction is true. The class previously
relied on the implicit copy/move members:

  - The implicit copy ctor copied _delete_file_on_destruction and
    _file_name verbatim, so two instances could end up racing to delete
    the same file.
  - The implicit move ctor moved _file_name (which leaves the moved-from
    string in an implementation-defined valid state) but only copied the
    bool flag, leaving the moved-from instance still claiming ownership.
    Whether the source destructor then attempted to delete the wrong file
    depended on std::string's moved-from representation.

Make the type non-copyable and add explicit noexcept move operations that
transfer ownership of _delete_file_on_destruction and clear it on the
source, so only the destination'

Implement sock_addr bind hook usermode tests (#5300)

* Add sock_addr bind hook usermode tests and fuzzer coverage

Add netebpfext usermode tests and libFuzzer coverage for the
CGROUP_SOCK_ADDR bind hook, mirroring the existing connect / recv-accept
/ listen test helpers.

- netebpf_ext_helper.h: add test_bind_ipv6 and test_cgroup_inet4/6_bind
  helpers. All test_* helpers take a const fwp_classify_parameters_t* and
  const_cast at the usersim boundary, enforcing immutability of the shared
  parameters object across reused v4/v6 calls (addresses @dthaler review
  feedback on #5300).
- Route the bind helpers through usersim_fwp_bind_ipv4/ipv6_by_callout so
  the legacy bind and CGROUP_SOCK_ADDR bind hooks -- which share the
  ALE_RESOURCE_ASSIGNMENT layer and default sublayer -- are disambiguated
  by callout key: test_bind_ipv4/6 target the legacy bind callout and
  test_cgroup_inet4/6_bind target the sock_addr bind callout (addresses
  @Alan-Jowett review feedback on #5300).
- netebpf

Fix flaky UDP thread/process affinity test assertions (#5383)

* Fix flaky UDP thread/process affinity test assertions

The bpf_get_thread_start_time and bpf_get_process_start_key tests
incorrectly assumed that WFP ALE_AUTH_CONNECT hooks run on the caller's
thread for UDP connections. This assumption was falsified on ARM64
NativeOnlyDebug where the classify ran on a worker thread.

Remove the protocol-conditional branches in run_thread_start_time_test
and run_process_start_key_test, replacing strict identity assertions
(exact TID/PID match) with validity checks (non-zero) for both TCP and
UDP. The WFP ALE_AUTH_CONNECT callout does not guarantee caller-thread
affinity for either protocol.

The bpf_get_current_pid_tgid test (BPF_PROG_TYPE_BIND on
FWPS_LAYER_ALE_RESOURCE_ASSIGNMENT_V4) is unchanged because that
layer does fire inline on the caller thread.

Use UserMode for SeAccessCheck calls evaluating user-mode callers (#5285)

* Use UserMode for SeAccessCheck calls evaluating user-mode callers

SeAccessCheck was called with KernelMode in ebpf_access_check,
_ebpf_driver_is_caller_privileged, and ebpf_drv.c. Using KernelMode
causes SeAccessCheck to always succeed, bypassing the actual DACL
check and mandatory integrity level enforcement.

Fix by changing to UserMode in both call sites. Additionally, fix the
security descriptor built by _ebpf_driver_build_privileged_security_descriptor
which was incomplete — it only had an ACE for the ebpfsvc SID and was
missing an owner, group, and ACEs for Administrators and SYSTEM. With
KernelMode this was masked; with UserMode the incomplete descriptor
caused access checks to fail.

The security descriptor now matches the device SDDL pattern:
- Owner: Administrators (S-1-5-32-544)
- Group: SYSTEM (S-1-5-18)
- DACL: ebpfsvc SID, Administrators, SYSTEM (all with GENERIC_ALL)

Bump external/ubpf to close ubpf_fuzzer ASAN crash (#5374)

* Bump external/ubpf to close ubpf_fuzzer ASAN crash

The fuzzer's `ubpf_get_helper_prototype` stub in
`libfuzzer/libfuzz_harness.cc` returned a default-constructed
`EbpfHelperPrototype{}` whose `.name` is a null pointer. Verifier
paths that assigned `.name` to a `std::string` then dereferenced
NULL, crashing `ubpf_fuzzer.exe`.

This bump picks up the upstream ubpf fix (iovisor/ubpf#794) that
makes the stub throw `std::runtime_error` instead, matching the
"not implemented" contract used by the sibling stubs in the same
file (`ubpf_parse_maps_section`, `ubpf_resolve_inner_map_references`,
`ubpf_get_map_descriptor`). PREVAIL has been null-tolerant since
vbpf/prevail `6f0384e3` ("Only Use Result From get_helper_prototype
when valid"); throwing is the correct contract for a stub that does
not implement helper functions.

  extracting listen-specific WFP fields (local address/port only).
- Add cgroup/listen4 and cgroup/listen6 section definitions.

Fix connect_redirect test cascading failures and overlapped I/O leak (#5095)

* Fix connect_redirect test cascading failures and overlapped I/O leak

Fixes #5094, #5096, #5105

connect_redirect_tests have a flaky failure pattern where one test
timeout causes cascading failures in subsequent tests. Root causes:

1. Policy map cleanup missing on exception - update_policy_map_and_test_
   connection() adds a policy map entry but only removes it at the end.
   When FAIL() throws, cleanup is skipped and stale entries cause the
   next test to unexpectedly pass traffic.

2. Overlapped I/O not cleaned up on timeout/error - completion functions
   don't cancel pending I/O, close event handles, or reset state flags
   when timeouts occur. This leaks I/O state across test phases.

3. Insufficient receive timeout - 2-second timeout too tight for CI.

- Add _policy_map_guard RAII class for automatic policy map cleanup
- Replace raw new/delete with std::unique_ptr for socket ownership
- Increase re

Add EverParse-based IOCTL message validation (#5081)

* Add EverParse-based IOCTL message validation

Add formal validation of IOCTL message structure using EverParse 3D
specification. The generated validator is compiled as a separate
translation unit in both user-mode and kernel-mode execution context
libraries, following the pattern used by nvlib in the Windows kernel.

Key changes:
- libs/ioctl_spec/EbpfProtocol.3d: EverParse 3D specification for all
  46 IOCTL operations (header validation, enum range checks, field
  offset ordering, context offset bounds)
- libs/ioctl_spec/ebpf_protocol_validator.c: Wrapper that includes the
  EverParse-generated code in a separate TU to avoid CRT/WDK header
  conflicts
- libs/ioctl_spec/ebpf_protocol_validator.h: Clean C header usable from
  both user-mode and kernel-mode code
- libs/ioctl_spec/ioctl_spec.vcxproj: Utility project for EverParse
  code generation (no library output)
- Validation call added to ebpf_core_invoke_protocol_handler()

Fix OOB access in _initialize_ebpf_programs_native on program count mismatch (#5152)

* Add regression test for OOB access in _initialize_ebpf_programs_native

Problem: _initialize_ebpf_programs_native iterates using count_of_programs
from a kernel IOCTL reply without validating it against programs.size()
(populated from PE section parsing). When these counts disagree, programs[i]
reads past the vector bounds, dereferencing a null/garbage pointer and
crashing with EXCEPTION_ACCESS_VIOLATION (0xC0000005).

Test: Simulates the count mismatch by emptying object->programs after
bpf_object__open (PE parsing) but before bpf_object__load (kernel IOCTL).
Uses SEH __try/__except to detect the access violation. Handles both
debug builds (STL iterator debugging) and release builds (raw null deref).

Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>

Allow sockops BPF programs to query the WFP flow_id (#4763)

* Allow sockops BPF programs to query the WFP flow_id

Resolves: #4764

Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>
Signed-off-by: Alan Jowett <alanjo@microsoft.com>

* Fix flow_id test: set interface_luid in lookup key and require success

The BPF program stores map entries keyed with ctx->interface_luid (non-zero
for loopback), but the test lookup key had interface_luid=0, causing the
hash map lookup to always fail. The if guard silently skipped validation.

Fix: set interface_luid to IF_TYPE_SOFTWARE_LOOPBACK (matching the pattern
used elsewhere in socket_tests.cpp) and change the if guard to REQUIRE so
lookup failure is caught.

Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>
Signed-off-by: Alan Jowett <alanjo@microsoft.com>

epoch: fix per-CPU epoch skew (published global epoch) + add regression tests (#4924)

* Add epoch skew hazard benchmark test

Adds a hidden Catch2 test that fails if epoch skew allows reclamation while a reader remains active in a newer epoch. Also updates epoch memory management documentation and includes a problem/fix write-up.

Signed-off-by: Alan Jowett <alan.jowett@microsoft.com>

* Fix epoch skew by publishing global epoch

Use a globally published epoch for both ebpf_epoch_enter() and retirement stamping to prevent epoch skew hazards under per-CPU lag. Update the regression test to avoid deadlock by not waiting for reclamation while holding an epoch.

Signed-off-by: Alan Jowett <alan.jowett@microsoft.com>

* Update epoch memory management doc for published epoch

Document the globally published epoch used for epoch entry and retirement stamping, and clarify that per-CPU current_epoch is a cached value that may lag until the propose/commit message is processed.

Signed-off-by: A

Consolidates the RISC-V 32-bit and 64-bit GNU/Clang port sources, fixes two
pre-existing assembly bugs discovered during testing, and hardens the build
infrastructure for both the regression suite and the CORE-V MCU example.

--- Port consolidation (RV32 GNU + Clang) ---

 - Delete ports/risc-v32/clang/src/ (8 .S files had no Clang-specific
 directives; diverged from GNU only due to missing bug fixes). The Clang
 port CMakeLists.txt now compiles from ../gnu/src/.
 - Change .global -> .weak for _tx_initialize_low_level in gnu/src/ to allow
 BSP-level override without a linker conflict (adopted from Clang port).
 - Create ports/risc-v32/common/tx_port_riscv32_common.h with all definitions
 shared between GNU and Clang ports. Reduce both tx_port.h files to thin
 wrappers.
 - Add a prominent comment in risc-v64/gnu/inc/tx_port.h explaining why
 LONG/ULONG are intentional

 Windows x64 port and regression suite

 This PR adds the Windows x64 (Win64) simulation port for both the standalone
 and SMP variants of ThreadX, along with the full CMake build and test
 infrastructure needed to run the regression suite on Windows.


 New ports

 Win64 standalone (ports/win64/vs_2022): self-contained Windows simulation
 port using Win32 threading primitives as virtual cores. Includes CMake
 integration, build/test scripts, and MSVC project files.

 Win64 SMP (ports/win64_smp/vs_2022): multi-core Windows simulation port.
 Supports up to 4 virtual cores backed by Windows host threads.


 Scheduler and timer improvements

 The initial port used coarse polling and synchronous SuspendThread/ResumeThread
 pairs throughout the scheduler hot path. Several rounds of optimization reduced
 the SMP regression suite runtime from ~150 s to ~78 s (-48%), with no
 regressions:

 - Replaced scheduler polling with an event-driven w

void  _tx_win32_profile_report(CHAR *label)
{
ULONG64  elapsed_ticks;

    elapsed_ticks =  _tx_win32_profile_time_get() - _tx_win32_profile.tx_win32_profile_start_ticks;

    printf("**** Win64 SMP Profile (%s) elapsed_ms=%.3f\n",
           label,
           _tx_win32_profile_ticks_to_ms(elapsed_ticks));
    printf("**** waits: scheduler=%lu/%.3fms run=%lu/%.3fms start=%lu/%.3fms start_ack=%lu/%.3fms sig_wake=%lu/%.3fms wake_ack=%lu/%.3fms isr=%lu/%.3fms isr_rdv=%lu/%.3fms timer=%lu/%.3fms\n",
           _tx_win32_profile.tx_win32_profile_scheduler_wait_count,
           _tx_win32_profile_ticks_to_ms(_tx_win32_profile.tx_win32_profile_scheduler_wait_ticks),
           _tx_win32_profile.tx_win32_profile_thread_run_wait_count,
           _tx_win32_profile_ticks_to_ms(_tx_win32_profile.tx_win32_profile_thread_run_wait_ticks),
           _tx_win32_profile.tx_win32_profile_thread_start_wait_count,
           _tx_win32_profile_ticks_to_ms(_tx_win32_profile.tx_win32_profile_thread_start_wait_ticks),
           _tx_win32_profile.tx_win32_profile_thread_start_ack_wait_count,
           _tx_win32_profile_ticks_to_ms(_tx_win32_profile.tx_win32_profile_thread_start_ack_wait_ticks),
           _tx_win32_profile.tx_win32_profile_run_signal_to_wake_count,
           _tx_win32_profile_ticks_to_ms(_tx_win32_profile.tx_win32_profile_run_signal_to_wake_ticks),
           _tx_win32_profile.tx_win32_profile_run_wake_to_ack_count,
           _tx_win32_profile_ticks_to_ms(_tx_win32_profile.tx_win32_profile_run_wake_to_ack_ticks),
           _tx_win32_profile.tx_win32_profile_isr_wait_count,
           _tx_win32_profile_ticks_to_ms(_tx_win32_profile.tx_win32_profile_isr_wait_ticks),
           _tx_win32_profile.tx_win32_profile_isr_rendezvous_wait_count,
           _tx_win32_profile_ticks_to_ms(_tx_win32_profile.tx_win32_profile_isr_rendezvous_wait_ticks),
           _tx_win32_profile.tx_win32_profile_timer_wait_count,
           _tx_win32_profile_ticks_to_ms(_tx_win32_profile.tx_win32_profile_timer_wait_ticks));
    printf("**** host ops: suspend=%lu/%.3fms resume=%lu/%.3fms reset=%lu/%.3fms reset_loops=%lu cs_spin=%lu/%.3fms yield=%lu/%.3fms\n",
           _tx_win32_profile.tx_win32_profile_suspend_count,
           _tx_win32_profile_ticks_to_ms(_tx_win32_profile.tx_win32_profile_suspend_ticks),
           _tx_win32_profile.tx_win32_profile_resume_count,
           _tx_win32_profile_ticks_to_ms(_tx_win32_profile.tx_win32_profile_resume_ticks),
           _tx_win32_profile.tx_win32_profile_semaphore_reset_count,
           _tx_win32_profile_ticks_to_ms(_tx_win32_profile.tx_win32_profile_semaphore_reset_ticks),
           _tx_win32_profile.tx_win32_profile_semaphore_reset_loops,
           _tx_win32_profile.tx_win32_profile_critical_section_spin_count,
           _tx_win32_profile_ticks_to_ms(_tx_win32_profile.tx_win32_profile_critical_section_spin_ticks),
           _tx_win32_profile.tx_win32_profile_yield_count,
           _tx_win32_profile_ticks_to_ms(_tx_win32_profile.tx_win32_profile_yield_ticks));
}

Added RISC-V board Bananapi BPI-F3 (SpacemiT K1 SoC) BSP Support  (#531)

* Add BananaPi BPI-F3 BSP support

Add RISC-V supervisor support to the rv64/gnu port and
provide a complete board support package for the BananaPi BPI-F3
(SpacemiT K1 SoC, X60 cores).

Port changes (risc-v64/gnu):
- Guard all CSR accesses with TX_RISCV_SMODE to select S-mode registers
  (sstatus/sepc/sie/sret) vs M-mode (mstatus/mepc/mie/mret) in
  context_save, context_restore, schedule, system_return,
  interrupt_control, and stack_build.
- Add S-mode TX_INT_ENABLE/TX_DISABLE and inline TX_RESTORE macros
  to tx_port.h.
- Add TX_RISCV_SMODE CMake option to CMakeLists.txt.

BananaPi BPI-F3 BSP (example_build/bananapi-f3):
- Boot flow: FSBL → OpenSBI (M-mode) → U-Boot (S-mode) → ThreadX
- S-mode trap handler with context save/restore integration

Add RISC-V supervisor support to the rv64/gnu port and
provide a complete board support package for the BananaPi BPI-F3
(SpacemiT K1 SoC, X60 cores).

Port changes (risc-v64/gnu):
- Guard all CSR accesses with TX_RISCV_SMODE to select S-mode registers
  (sstatus/sepc/sie/sret) vs M-mode (mstatus/mepc/mie/mret) in
  context_save, context_restore, schedule, system_return,
  interrupt_control, and stack_build.
- Add S-mode TX_INT_ENABLE/TX_DISABLE and inline TX_RESTORE macros
  to tx_port.h.
- Add TX_RISCV_SMODE CMake option to CMakeLists.txt.

BananaPi BPI-F3 BSP (example_build/bananapi-f3):
- Boot flow: FSBL → OpenSBI (M-mode) → U-Boot (S-mode) → ThreadX
- S-mode trap handler with context save/restore integration
- SBI legacy ecall timer at 10 Hz (24 MHz timebase)
- PLIC driver with S-mode context, stale-IRQ drain, and callbacks
- PXA-compatible UART0 console (115200 8N1)
- Linke

Fix an options hash Oj knows no key of detaching a Rails encoder (#1093)

* Fix an options hash Oj knows no key of detaching a Rails encoder

ActiveSupport 8.1 caches two encoders inside json_encoder=, one built
with no options and one built with {escape: false}. encoder_new() took a
non-empty options hash as reason enough to snapshot oj_default_options
into the encoder, and rails_set_encoder() calls json_encoder= before it
writes ActiveSupport::JSON::Encoding.time_precision into those defaults.
The escape: false encoder therefore froze sec_prec at 9 while the
option-less one, made lazy by #1049, went on reading the live defaults.
Since both read the same optimized class table, to_json(escape: false)
dumped optimized timestamps with 9 fractional digits where every other
path used the configured precision.

Oj has never had an :escape option. parse_options_cb() ignores a key it
does not recognize, so the only effect {escape: false} ever had was to
detach the encoder from the defaults.

Fix the wab mode time load being an offset out on Windows (#1088)

mktime() stood in for timegm() on Windows, subtracting the epoch
expressed in local time to cancel the timezone offset out. The Microsoft
CRT returns -1 for any time before the epoch, so east of UTC the local
1970-01-01 00:00 is itself before the epoch and the correction term
became -(-1), leaving the offset in place and adding a second. In JST
"2017-01-05T23:58:07.123456789Z" loaded back as 14:58:08.

The same -1 also applies to the date being parsed, so every time before
1970 loaded wrong on Windows in any timezone, including UTC.

Compute the days directly so the IS_WINDOWS branch can go away and both
platforms run the same code. time_as_sec() is added to util.c as the
inverse of sec_as_time(), which the dump side of wab.c already uses.

The limits are applied by wrapping the parser function table: safe.c
replaces the add_* and open_* slots of ARRAY_FUN and OBJECT_FUN with
counting versions that call what was there before. The option setters of

opt_create_id_set() puts add_str back, so an option set after the parser
was built takes the counting out again for that kind of value, with

    parser.decimal = :float

way, since parser_safe() does not forward anything but the four max_*
keys.

replaces unless the slot already holds the wrappe

Every JSON object key shorter than CACHE_MAX_KEY is interned through
cache_intern(), and the bucket it lands in is decided by hash_calc() in
cache.c, an almost-Murmur hash seeded with nothing but the key length.
intern.c carries a second copy of the same function for the class cache.

precompute keys that all land in one bucket. Collisions are resolved
with an unbounded list that is walked on every insert and every lookup,

variant walks that chain holding the cache mutex, so other threads block
as well, and the entries live in a process wide cache that survives many
GC cycles, so later unrelated parses stay slow too. This reaches every
entry point that interns keys with the default options: Oj.load,
Oj::Parser, and JSON.parse under Oj.mimic_JSON, which forces cache_keys.

Hold onto the Ruby objects in the default options (#1035)

* Hold onto the Ruby objects in the default options

The default options are a plain C global, so the classes of the
hash_class, array_class, and ignore options and the regexps and classes
of the match_string option can not be reached by the GC and were
collected while the defaults still referred to them. Loading with a
default match_string that has a Regexp key segfaults after a collection
since matching calls the regexp.

Rebuild an array of those objects whenever the defaults change and keep
it in an instance variable of the Oj module. A mark function on a hidden
object works on CRuby but TruffleRuby never runs it, and a C global
registered with rb_gc_register_address() does not follow the values
assigned to it later, while an instance variable is a reference every
engine can follow.

Fix per-call memory leaks and default corruption in option handling (#1029)

Passing create_id, ignore, only, or except to Oj.load / Oj.dump leaked a heap
copy of the option on every call, and changing Oj.default_options[:create_id]
leaked the previous default string. A per-call options struct is a copy of
oj_default_options, so oj_parse_options allocated a fresh buffer into it that
nothing ever freed; the default create_id was likewise replaced without
freeing the old one. Confirmed O(n) under Valgrind (e.g. 500 Oj.load(...,
create_id:) calls -> 500 lost blocks; likewise ignore/only/except via Oj.dump
and 500 Oj.default_options={create_id:...} changes).

For only/except/ignore there was also a use-after-free: the per-call copy's
pointer still aliased the default-owned buffer, so parse_options_cb freed the
default's buffer, and the reused address then read back as the "new" default
value, silently mutating Oj.default_options.

Fix illegal instruction error on CPUs without SSE4.2 support (#993)

* Fix illegal instruction error on CPUs without SSE4.2 support

This fixes issue #989 where oj 3.16.13 crashes with "Illegal instruction"
on CPUs that don't support SSE4.2.

The problem was that enabling -msse4.2 at compile time based on compiler
support caused prebuilt gems to include SSE4.2 instructions even when the
target CPU doesn't support them.

Solution:
- Use runtime CPU detection to select the appropriate SIMD implementation
- Detection happens once during library initialization (no per-parse overhead)
- Cross-platform support: GCC/Clang (__builtin_cpu_supports) and MSVC (__cpuid)
- Function-level target attributes enable SIMD code without global flags
- Portable macros (OJ_PREFETCH, OJ_CTZ, OJ_UNLIKELY) for cross-compiler support

This is similar to the approach used by ruby/json for SIMD detection.

Avoid overflow in Levenshtein distance calculations.

levenshtein() and levenshtein_less_equal() let the caller specify
the insertion, deletion, and substitution costs, and
fuzzystrmatch's corresponding SQL functions accept any 32-bit
integer for each.  Since the distances are calculated with 32-bit
arithmetic, large costs can cause overflows, thereby producing
nonsensical results.  Certain inputs to levenshtein_less_equal()
can even cause out-of-bounds writes.  To fix, use 64-bit arithmetic
instead, and error whenever the final result won't fit in the
returned 32-bit integer.

We may want to teach these functions to reject negative costs, too,
but that didn't seem appropriate for a security fix, and therefore
it is left as a future exercise.

  to avoid repeatedly enumerating the same directory when resolving K

Merge branch 'exp-work': ktimer, fast uaccess, TTY canon editing, coverage TUI

Seventy-one commits since the divergence from master (132 files,
+8812/-941). Four roughly equal pillars: a kernel-core perf arc
(timer rework, AVL bintree tuning, a wakeup-latency fix), an mm arc
(complete user-mapping bookkeeping, CoW-OOM recovery, a lightweight
on-fault uaccess path with honest -ENOMEM), a TTY/console
correctness arc culminating in the canonical line-editing redesign,
and a test-infrastructure arc that folds all four test types plus
coverage collection into one runner and adds an ncurses coverage
viewer.

The O(N)-per-tick linked-list timer scan is replaced by an AVL tree
keyed by absolute expiry tick, with a cached earliest-timer pointer
that makes the common per-tick check O(1) with no IRQ-disable;
insert, cancel and expiry processing are O(log N) with bounded
IRQ-off time per expired timer. task_set_wakeup_timer() widens to
u64 ti

TEST_F(console_test, tab_marks_cleared_when_row_scrolls_away)
{
   /*
    * A row that scrolls off and is reused must not keep its old tab marks: the
    * stale mark would make a later backspace over a *real* character jump like
    * a tab. Put a tab on the bottom row, scroll it away, type fresh text on the
    * reused row, then erase one char -- it must be a plain one-cell backspace.
    */
   const char bs = (char)t->c_term.c_cc[VERASE];

   set_cursor_to(4, 0);
   console_write("\t");              /* tab on the bottom row, ends at col 7 */
   console_write("\r\n");            /* scroll: bottom row reused and cleared */
   console_write("abcdefgh");        /* 8 fresh chars on the reused row       */
   console_write(&bs, 1);            /* erase the last one                    */

   check_screen_vs_expected(R"(
      +--------------------+
      |                    |
      |                    |
      |                    |
      |                    |
      |abcdefg$            |
      +--------------------+
   )");
}

wallet: register scriptpubkey watches at startup

init_wallet_scriptpubkey_watches walks every HD key (BIP32 + BIP86) up
to {bip32,bip86}_max_index + keyscan_gap and arms a watch for each
form, so bwatch can report deposits from the very first block it
scans.  wallet_get_newindex does the same for fresh keys, keeping
coverage as the wallet grows.

The per-UTXO watch on unconfirmed change is now redundant (the
perennial per-key watch already covers that scriptpubkey), so drop it.

Co-authored-by: Cursor <cursoragent@cursor.com>

lightningd: only run watchman under --experimental-bwatch

The flag is registered by the bwatch plugin, not lightningd, so peek
at the parsed configvars.  Without it ld->watchman stays NULL and the
watchman_* entry points are no-ops, leaving chain_topology as the only
chain watcher: bwatch and the legacy path must not race each other.

The bwatch pytests opt in explicitly (with rescan=0) instead of
enabling bwatch globally.

wallet: read UTXO state from our_outputs

With every writer dual-writing since the previous two commits, flip
the readers: all UTXO queries (listfunds, coin selection, reservations,
onchaind close info) now come from our_outputs, and the legacy-only
read helpers (wallet_stmt2output, gather_utxos, db_get_unspent_utxos)
are deleted.

our_output_row_to_utxo replaces wallet_stmt2output, using channel_dbid
to discriminate HD outputs from channel-close outputs, and
wallet_get_spendable_utxos centralizes the unspent+unreserved query
that wallet_find_utxo and wallet_has_funds previously duplicated.

migrate_setup_coinmoves keeps reading the legacy table directly: that
migration runs at v25.09, before our_outputs exists.

wallet: handle reorgs for our_outputs/our_txs by hand

The legacy tables rely on their blocks(height) ON DELETE SET NULL
foreign keys to mark rows unconfirmed/unspent when a block is reorged
out.  our_outputs/our_txs deliberately carry no blocks FK (bwatch does
not maintain a blocks table), so block disconnect and rollback must
demote their blockheight/spendheight fields explicitly.

Demote, never delete: a row also carries state the chain cannot
re-deliver (reserved_til, onchaind close metadata), and this path runs
not just on real reorgs but on every startup, when chaintopology
invalidates its rescan window.  Rediscovery re-promotes the row via
wallet_add_our_output / wallet_transaction_add; a tx that never
re-confirms just stays unconfirmed and unspendable.

wallet: handle bwatch wallet/utxo spend notifications

When bwatch_got_utxo() records a wallet output, it arms an outpoint
watch owned by wallet/utxo/<txid>:<outnum>.  This adds the receiving
end of that watch: the dispatch entry plus the found/revert handlers.

On watch_found (a tx consumed the outpoint): mark the output spent in
our_outputs, store the spending tx in our_txs, and emit a withdrawal
coin movement.  On watch_revert (a reorg removed that tx): clear
spendheight so the UTXO is spendable again.

void migrate_backfill_bwatch_tables(struct lightningd *ld UNNEEDED, struct db *db)
{
	struct db_stmt *stmt;

	stmt = db_prepare_v2(db,
		SQL("INSERT INTO our_outputs "
		    "(txid, outnum, blockheight, txindex, scriptpubkey, satoshis, "
		    " spendheight, reserved_til, keyindex, channel_dbid, peer_id, "
		    " commitment_point, option_anchors, csv) "
		    "SELECT "
		    "  prev_out_tx, "
		    "  prev_out_index, "
		    "  COALESCE(confirmation_height, 0), "
		    "  CASE "
		    "    WHEN confirmation_height IS NULL THEN 0 "
		    "    WHEN is_in_coinbase = 1 THEN 0 "
		    "    ELSE 1 "
		    "  END, "
		    "  scriptpubkey, "
		    "  value, "
		    "  spend_height, "
		    "  COALESCE(reserved_til, 0), "
		    "  CASE WHEN channel_id IS NULL THEN keyindex ELSE NULL END, "
		    "  channel_id, "
		    "  peer_id, "
		    "  commitment_point, "
		    "  option_anchor_outputs, "
		    "  csv_lock "
		    "FROM outputs "
		    "WHERE scriptpubkey IS NOT NULL "
		    "ON CONFLICT(txid,outnum) DO NOTHING;"));
	db_exec_prepared_v2(take(stmt));

	stmt = db_prepare_v2(db,
		SQL("INSERT INTO our_txs "
		    "(txid, blockheight, txindex, rawtx) "
		    "SELECT id, blockheight, COALESCE(txindex, 0), rawtx "
		    "FROM transactions "
		    "WHERE blockheight IS NOT NULL AND rawtx IS NOT NULL "
		    "ON CONFLICT(txid) DO NOTHING;"));
	db_exec_prepared_v2(take(stmt));
}

wallet: record bwatch-discovered wallet outputs

Add the wallet helpers and watch handlers that turn a bwatch
scriptpubkey match into our_txs and our_outputs rows.  They validate
the matching output, notify invoice accounting, record confirmed
deposits, and install watches for later spends.

The watch_revert handler demotes the rows back to unconfirmed (the 0
sentinel) rather than deleting them: a row also carries state a
rediscovery cannot restore (reserved_til, onchaind close metadata),
and the still-armed watches re-promote it if the tx confirms again.
This matches the legacy tables, whose blocks(height) foreign keys
demote rows to NULL when the block row is removed.

Unlike got_utxo(), this path does not write transaction_annotations:
nothing reads per-transaction annotations anymore, so only the legacy
scanner keeps populating them (for downgrade, like the other legacy
tables).

path alongside got_utxo() and

wallet: Update the max_index cache when issuing new addresses

The write-through cache added for the address max_index was only kept in
sync in wallet_can_spend(). wallet_get_newindex() still read and wrote
the bip32_max_index/bip86_max_index db vars directly, leaving the
in-memory cache stale after every newaddr. Since listaddresses and the
rescan window now read from that cache, freshly issued addresses were
invisible until the next restart (and wallet_can_spend could even write a
stale, lower value back to the db).

Route all reads and writes through wallet_max_addr_index() and
wallet_set_max_addr_index() so the cache and the db never diverge.

Add support for the Uruguayan national eID card (cédula de identidad)

The Uruguayan electronic ID card (cédula de identidad) is a Gemalto
"Classic V4" IAS/ECC platform card that OpenSC did not recognize
(opensc-tool -n reported an unsupported card). Its only middleware is
the closed-source Gemalto Classic Client, so there was no open stack
for it.

The subset of the card exposed over the contact interface is plain
ISO 7816, so the card is supported by a dedicated driver
(card-cedulauy.c) built on the generic iso7816 operations, paired
with a synthetic PKCS#15 emulator (pkcs15-cedulauy.c), following the
model of card-esteid2018.c.

card-cedulauy.c:

  - matches the ATR under a mask: TA1 and the historical bytes
    carrying the platform version and batch differ between card
    batches (mask suggested by Nicolás Gutiérrez, whose card from
    another batch differs in exactly those bytes);
  - selects the IAS application by AID at init -- nothing on the card
    is accessible before tha

Fix uninitialized encaps_derand pointer dereference for NTRU KEMs (#2460)

* Fix uninitialized encaps_derand pointer dereference for NTRU KEMs

The six NTRU KEM constructors (hps2048509, hps2048677, hps4096821,
hps40961229, hrss701, hrss1373) did not initialize the encaps_derand
function pointer in OQS_KEM, and OQS_KEM_encaps_derand did not guard
against a NULL function pointer. Calling OQS_KEM_encaps_derand on an
NTRU KEM dereferenced uninitialized heap memory, causing a crash.

Three layers of fix:

1. Add explicit OQS_KEM_ntru_<scheme>_encaps_derand stubs returning
   OQS_ERROR (matching the existing keypair_derand stubs), and wire
   them into the NTRU constructors.

2. NULL-check the function pointer in all five OQS_KEM_* API wrappers
   in src/kem/kem.c as defense in depth against future omissions.

3. Switch all KEM constructors from OQS_MEM_malloc to OQS_MEM_calloc
   so any unset field is guaranteed NULL, making the API NULL check
   reliable. The jinja template in scripts/cop

Add OQS_SIG_STFL_keygen_and_sign_supported() for runtime detection (#2434)

* Guard trailing_1_bits with OQS_ALLOW_LMS_KEY_AND_SIG_GEN

The static helper trailing_1_bits in hss_keygen.c is only called from
inside the OQS_ALLOW_LMS_KEY_AND_SIG_GEN block, so configurations that
disable stateful key/signature generation (e.g. the
alpine-no-stfl-key-sig-gen CI job) trip -Wunused-function. The warning
was latent until the ci-alpine-amd64 image refresh brought in a CMake
new enough (>= 3.24) for CMAKE_COMPILE_WARNING_AS_ERROR to actually add
-Werror, turning it into a build failure.

Wrap the definition in the same #ifdef as its sole caller.

column6:
perf(lf): drop double-precision sqrt from FSK demod hot path

The build targets the Cortex-M4F single-precision FPU (-mfpu=fpv4-sp-d16),
which has no double-precision hardware. goertzel_mag() used sqrt() (double):
the float result was promoted to double for the call and converted back, and
a software double-sqrt routine ran -- twice per decoded bit.

The bit decision only compares the two Goertzel outputs, and power is
monotonic with magnitude, so the sqrt is unnecessary. goertzel_power()
returns the squared magnitude and fsk_feed() compares that directly. This
also removes a latent sqrt(NaN): the magnitude argument can round slightly
negative near zero signal, which sqrt() turned into NaN (and NaN comparisons
make the bit decision unreliable); comparing the raw power is well-defined.

The old goertzel_mag() had no callers anywhere and was not declared in the
header, so it is removed rather than kept.

Shared by all FSK readers (HID Prox, ioProx, Pyramid): bit decisions are
identical,

Add Jablotron LF tag support (read, emulate, write to T55xx)

Jablotron uses differential biphase (inverted) at RF/64, 64-bit frames:
  bits  0-15: 0xFFFF preamble
  bits 16-55: 40-bit data (5 bytes), bit 16 must be 0
  bits 56-63: 8-bit checksum = (sum of data bytes) XOR 0x3A

Firmware:
  - rfid/nfctag/lf/protocols/jablotron.c  - encoder/decoder codec
  - rfid/nfctag/lf/utils/diphase.c        - inverted-biphase state machine
    (shared util, reusable by other diphase protocols)
  - rfid/reader/lf/lf_jablotron_data.c    - GPIO-interval reader path
  - app_cmd.c: JABLOTRON_SCAN, JABLOTRON_WRITE_TO_T55XX,
                JABLOTRON_SET_EMU_ID, JABLOTRON_GET_EMU_ID
  - tag_base_type.h: TAG_TYPE_JABLOTRON enum
  - t55xx.h: T5577_JABLOTRON_CONFIG (DIPHASE modulation, RF/64)
  - lf_tag_em.c: load callback, factory-default data, save callback

Python CLI (software/script/):
  - lf jablotron read               - scan a real tag
  - lf jablotron write --id         - clone onto T55xx
  - lf jabl

Add surface position decoding (Type Code 5-8).

Aircraft on the ground transmit surface position messages with a different
CPR encoding than airborne positions. The key challenge is that surface CPR
requires a reference position within 45 nautical miles for unambiguous
decoding.

Instead of requiring users to configure their location, we automatically
compute a reference by averaging all successfully decoded airborne positions.
This works because if you can receive surface traffic from an airport, you
almost certainly receive airborne traffic too.

Implementation:
- Parse surface position fields: movement (ground speed), ground track
- Add decodeCPRSurface() for local CPR decoding with reference position
- Update reference position average after each airborne position decode
- Display surface positions with altitude 0 in interactive mode
- Surface messages are ignored until a reference position is established

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

decodeMovementField(int movement) {
    if (movement == 0) return -1;           /* Not available */
    if (movement == 1) return 0;            /* Stopped (< 0.125 kt) */
    if (movement <= 8) return (movement - 2) * 0.125 + 0.125;  /* 0.125-1 kt */
    if (movement <= 12) return (movement - 9) * 0.25 + 1;      /* 1-2 kt */
    if (movement <= 38) return (movement - 13) * 0.5 + 2;      /* 2-15 kt */
    if (movement <= 93) return (movement - 39) + 15;           /* 15-70 kt */
    if (movement <= 108) return (movement - 94) * 2 + 70;      /* 70-100 kt */
    if (movement <= 123) return (movement - 109) * 5 + 100;    /* 100-175 kt */
    return 175;  /* >= 175 kt */
}

Add fast syndrome-based bit error correction.

Based on the implementation approach from malcolm-dump1090 fork.

This commit introduces a precomputed syndrome lookup table for
O(log n) bit error correction, replacing the O(n)/O(n^2) brute
force approach.

What is a syndrome?
------------------
When we compute CRC on a received message and XOR with the
transmitted CRC, we get the "syndrome". For valid messages,
syndrome = 0. For corrupted messages, the syndrome depends
only on which bits were flipped (not the message content),
thanks to CRC linearity.

Implementation:
- Precompute syndromes for all single-bit and two-bit error
  patterns (excluding first 5 bits which are the DF type)
- Sort table by syndrome for binary search
- On receive, compute syndrome and look it up in table
- If found, flip the indicated bits to fix the message

This is especially useful in aggressive mode where we attempt
to correct 2-bit errors: the O(n^2) brute force becomes O(log n).

ci/uprobe: Add Go integration test

Add a CI-only gadget attaching uprobes to a "main.target" Go function in
several Go binaries shipped in a locally built test image, to check that
uprobe symbol resolution keeps working for Go binaries built with
different Go versions and different linking and stripping options.

The workload image contains the same program built with Go 1.25 and
Go 1.26, each in a normal, PIE, linker-stripped (-ldflags='-s -w') and
strip(1)-ed variant. A single builder stage is used and the additional
Go toolchains are fetched through GOTOOLCHAIN, so only one golang image
is pulled. The image is built by "make -C gadgets ci/uprobe/workload-image"
and is not pushed anywhere; the mechanism is generic and picks up any
ci/<gadget>/workload/Dockerfile.

The test only runs with the docker runtime: the workload image is only
available to the local Docker daemon and what is tested here does not
depend on the container runtime.

The gadget generates one uprobe section per bin

gadgets/profile_cpu: add --gpu-idle-only GPU-starvation profiler

Add an optional --gpu-idle-only filter that turns profile_cpu into a
GPU-starvation profiler. When enabled, a stack sample is only recorded if
the sampled process currently owns GPU memory (per the gpu-ebpf-bridge
gpu_per_pid map) and its primary GPU is underutilized (SM utilization below
--gpu-util-max-pct) at that instant. The flamegraph then shows exactly the
CPU code that runs while the GPU the process paid for sits idle.

Because it is sampling-based, it has no dependence on the bridge poll
interval and therefore also surfaces "many small gaps" starvation (e.g. a
per-frame CPU preprocessing step keeping an inference GPU at ~50% duty
cycle), which the recency-based trace_gpu_starvation gadget cannot detect.

The pinned bridge maps and CO-RE helpers are shared via
<gadget/gpu_bridge_maps.h>. When the filter is off (the default) the maps
are declared but never read, so profile_cpu still loads on hosts without
the bridg

gadgets/trace_gpu_starvation: add finish_task_switch GPU-starvation tracer

Add a new gadget that detects GPU starvation: a process holds GPU
memory but its GPU sits idle while one of its threads keeps burning
CPU, which is the signature of a pipeline that is CPU-bound in the code
path meant to feed the GPU.

The gadget joins two signals:
- the per-process GPU metrics published by the in-repo gpu-ebpf-bridge
  daemon (VRAM held, and which device the process's memory lives on),
  and

to the JS host. When the Promise settles, JS calls io_resume_eval to
restore the suspended coro and re-enter the eval loop.

- io_resume_eval WASM export with chained await support
- JS-side resumeIfAwaiting() + pendingAsyncResolve callback
- Fixed coro save to use active coroutine (not self) so try()
  across suspend/resume works correctly with child coro frame swap

Replace hand-wrapped DOM CFunctions with a generic bridge that lets Io
code call any JS object and JS code send messages to any Io object.

handles. See agents/IoJsBridge.md for full design documentation.

Replace special form name list with isLazyArgs flag on CFunction

The iterative evaluator pre-evaluates message arguments for performance,
but special forms (if, while, foreach, etc.) need lazy evaluation. The
previous approach used a hardcoded list of ~20 symbol names, which failed
for aliases like `false.elseif := Object getSlot("if")` — the CFunction
was `if` but the message name `elseif` wasn't in the list, causing args
to be pre-evaluated (broke REPL launch).

Now each CFunction carries an `isLazyArgs` flag set once at VM init.
Since `getSlot` returns the same CFunction object (not a clone), any
alias automatically inherits the flag. This also fixes `./io` launching
without arguments (the if/then/elseif chain in Z_CLI.io).

Add hybrid reference counting infrastructure (disabled by default)

RC layer for the garbage collector, gated behind COLLECTOR_USE_REFCOUNT.
When enabled, promptly reclaims short-lived objects (especially for-loop
counter Numbers) via refcount tracking and drain, keeping the freed list
populated and avoiding calloc. Mark/sweep GC remains as backup for cycles.

GC library changes:
- refCount field on CollectorMarker (conditional on ifdef)
- RC increment in Collector_value_addingRefTo_
- RC decrement and enqueue in Collector_value_removingRefTo_
- Deferred free list (rcEnqueue/rcDrainFreeList) with safety guards
- inSweep flag to suppress RC frees during sweep phase

IoVM integration:
- IOUNREF macro for explicit reference release
- Slot overwrite decrement in IoObject_inlineSetSlot_to_ (no drain)
- Cascading decrement in IoObject_willFree via PHASH_FOREACH
- Bounded memory growth check in Collector_newMarker

Benchmarks with RC enabled: 1.5x faster on for(i,1,1M,i+1), ~7%
regression on

Block locals pooling for method call optimization

Reuse blockLocals objects across block activations instead of cloning
a new localsProto each time. Pool of 1 entry is returned on block
RETURN and reclaimed on next activation (PHash cleaned, slots rebound).

Key fixes for correctness:
- IoState_stackRetain_ pooled blockLocals after taking from pool,
  preventing GC sweep during IoCall_with allocation
- Do NOT pool blockLocals in TCO path — Call object references old
  blockLocals as sender, and relayStopStatus needs its slots alive
- Mark pooled blockLocals in IoCoroutine_mark for GC safety
- Cache Call tag/proto on IoState for inline allocation

Also adds fast path for trivial method bodies (single cached literal
like nil/true/number): skip entire block activation and return the
cached result directly.

Benchmarks (500K iterations, release build):
  Trivial method:     7.5s master → 0.8s stackless (9.4x faster)
  Method with args:  20.0s master → 2.0s stackless (10x faster)

GC-managed eval frames: IoEvalFrame as IoObject with pooled allocation

Convert IoEvalFrame from a manually-allocated C struct to a GC-managed
IoObject. Frames are now collector-tracked, enabling grab-pointer
continuation capture (no deep copy) and simplified coroutine marking.

Phase 0 - Mechanical rename:
- Introduce FRAME_DATA(frame) macro and IoEvalFrameData typedef
- Convert all frame->field to fd->field across 19 source files

Phase 1 - IoEvalFrame as IoObject:
- typedef IoObject IoEvalFrame; data payload behind IoObject_dataPointer
- Proto/tag/mark/free lifecycle following IoCall pattern
- Continuations use grab-pointer capture; copy method for snapshots
- IoCoroutine mark simplified to single IoObject_shouldMarkIfNonNull
- Remove manual frame pool from IoState; remove multiShot from continuations
- Exclude dead IoState_iterative_fast.c from build

Phase 2 - Performance recovery:
- Add 256-entry IoObject frame pool to IoState
- pushFrame_ reuses pooled frames (memset reset); pop

Add Continuation asMap serialization and frame introspection

Implement Continuation asMap method that produces a structured Map
representation of the captured frame stack. Each frame is serialized
with its state machine state, message code (reparseable), flags,
argument evaluation state, object type info, block locals slots,
Call stop status, and control flow parameters (loop counters, branch
messages, etc.).

Also add IoEvalFrame_stateName() for human-readable state names,
and Continuation introspection methods: frameCount, frameStates,
frameMessages. These are building blocks toward full continuation
serialization/deserialization.

30/30 C tests, 230 Io tests (3 pre-existing failures only).

Implement tail call optimization through if() branches: when if() is the
last message in a chain, evaluate the selected branch in-place instead of
pushing a child frame. This enables TCO for the common recursive pattern
`if(n <= 0, acc, recurse(n - 1, acc))`.
