stop status across in-place if optimization + TCO. Without this, the ?
operator's relayStopStatus would lose its RETURN/CONTINUE status when TCO
replaces frame->call. The RETURN handler now checks both frame->call and
frame->savedCall.

Eliminate C stack recursion: fully iterative eval with error safety

Remove inRecursiveEval flag — all evaluation now routes through the
iterative eval loop when currentFrame is set. A bootstrap-only recursive
fallback remains for VM initialization (before the first eval loop starts).

Key changes:
- Replace IoState_handleStopStatus_ with IoState_unwindFramesForError_
  which respects isNestedEvalRoot boundaries (prevents stale frame
  pointers when coro switch + nested eval combine)
- Control flow primitives (if, while, for, loop) use iterative path
  exclusively; bootstrap fallback only when !state->currentFrame
- Add error-safety checks (errorRaised return-early) across CFunctions:
  IoList, IoFile, IoMap, IoSeq, IoDate, IoDirectory, IoNumber, IoObject
- Remove libcoroutine entirely (no C stack switching needed)
- Add shouldExit check in eval loop for System exit support
- Track nestedEvalDepth in coroutine eval loop
- Add special forms: repeat, do, lexicalDo, foreachSlot,
  cpuSeco

Replace C stack recursion with heap-allocated frames to enable first-class
continuations and portable coroutines without platform-specific assembly.

- Iterative eval loop with frame state machine (IoState_iterative.c)
- Control flow primitives (if, while, for, loop) as frame manipulations
- First-class continuations via callcc with frame stack copy/restore
- Frame-based coroutines (no setjmp/longjmp, no ucontext, no fibers)
- Io-level exceptions bridged to eval loop via rawSignalException
- 13/13 tests passing including callcc and exception handling

Add continuation-capable iterative evaluator

This commit introduces a C-stack-independent evaluator that enables
first-class continuations, serializable execution state, and
network-portable coroutines.

## New Components

- IoEvalFrame: Frame structure for explicit evaluation stack
  * Replaces C recursion with explicit state machine

Two independent bugs in the bundled widget library made the curses UI
fall apart on modern ncurses. Both are misuse of the ncurses API on our
side, not a change in ncurses behaviour.

1) Menus and forms were posted onto stdscr.

   wdg_input, wdg_list and wdg_file built their menu/form sub-window with
   a geometry that does not fit inside its parent, e.g.

     mwin = newwin(mrows, MAX(mcols, c - 4), y + 1, x + 2);
     set_menu_sub(m, derwin(mwin, mrows + 1, mcols, 1, 1));

   The sub-window needs mrows + 2 lines but the parent only has mrows, so
   derwin() returns NULL. Passing NULL to set_menu_sub()/set_form_sub() is
   not an error for ncurses: it normalises the NULL sub-window to stdscr,
   so the widget content is drawn full-screen on stdscr instead of inside
   its own box. The next refresh of stdscr then paints over the whole
   panel stack.

Enforce LF line endings via .gitattributes and normalize existing files (#550)

## Summary

The repo declares `end_of_line = lf` in `.editorconfig`, but nothing
**enforced** it at the git level (no `.gitattributes`,
`core.autocrlf=false`). As a result, 12 tracked files had drifted to
CRLF or mixed line endings in the committed blobs, in violation of the
policy.

This PR adds the missing enforcement and normalizes the offenders.

## Changes (one theme per commit)

1. **Add `.gitattributes`** — `* text=auto eol=lf` so git normalizes
line endings on commit/checkout regardless of contributor OS, editor, or
tooling; `*.db3`/`*.png` marked `binary`. Also cross-references the
enforcement in the `sqlitecpp-coding-standards` skill.
2. **Normalize test sources** — `tests/Database_test.cpp`,
`tests/Transaction_test.cpp`.
3. **Normalize build/CMake config** — `meson_options.txt`,
`examples/example2/CMakeLists.txt`, `cmake/SQLiteCppConfig.cmake.in`,
`subprojects/.gitignore`.

action: allow Close and Kill while window switching

actions_run() drops every action other than NextWindow and
PreviousWindow while input_mode is LAB_INPUT_STATE_CYCLE. That makes it
impossible to bind, for example, A-q to Close and delete windows without
first releasing Alt to dismiss the window switcher.

Replace the hard-coded pair of allowed actions with a small whitelist and
add Close and Kill to it. Neither changes focus, opens a menu nor starts
an interactive move/resize, so neither can fight with the switcher's
focus override.

Actions run while the switcher is up now act on the view highlighted in
the OSD rather than on the still-active view, which is the window the
user is looking at.

Also name the rejected action in the log message, which is more useful
now that the set of accepted actions is no longer a fixed pair.

mme: DNS-based SGW/PGW selection per 3GPP TS 29.303 (c-ares)

Select the SGW by TAI-FQDN and the PGW by APN-FQDN using S-NAPTR
(NAPTR -> SRV -> A / NAPTR -> A) as described in 3GPP TS 29.303,
resolved asynchronously with c-ares integrated into the MME main
loop (sockets in ogs_pollset, timeouts via ogs_timer; no threads,
no blocking).

The feature is inert unless a new `mme.dns` section is configured:
without it (or without c-ares at build time) the static
gtpc.client.sgwc/smf selection is used unchanged.

Flow: mme_gtp_send_create_session_request() defers the CSR while
resolution is in flight; MME_EVENT_DNS_RESOLVED applies the result
(sgw_ue_switch_to_sgw() before any S11 TEID exists; PGW address
injected into the PGW S5/S8 F-TEID, after the HSS-provided
MIP6-Agent-Info but before the static PGW list) and sends the CSR.
On any DNS failure or guard-timer expiry the MME falls back to the
static configuration with a warning.

- Applies to initial attach and UE-requested PDN connectivity

Fix Android timed thread join with helper thread + condvar

Replace the blocking pthread_join fallback with a proper timed
implementation. Android Bionic lacks pthread_clockjoin_np, so we
spawn a helper thread that performs the join and signals a condvar.
The caller waits on the condvar with pthread_cond_timedwait, which
Bionic fully supports with CLOCK_MONOTONIC.

On timeout, ownership of the heap-allocated context transfers to the
helper thread, which cleans up after the target thread eventually
exits. This ensures correct CHIAKI_ERR_TIMEOUT semantics needed by
callers like discovery.

io_uring_enter: implement decoding of extended argument structures

The io_uring_enter syscall supports extended argument structures when
IORING_ENTER_EXT_ARG or IORING_ENTER_EXT_ARG_REG flags are set.  When
IORING_ENTER_EXT_ARG is set, the sigset argument is actually a pointer
to struct io_uring_getevents_arg containing sigmask, timespec, and
minimum wait time.  When IORING_ENTER_EXT_ARG_REG is set, the sigset
argument is a byte offset into a registered wait region in kernel
memory.

* src/io_uring.c (print_io_uring_getevents_arg): New function to
decode struct io_uring_getevents_arg.
(SYS_FUNC(io_uring_enter)): Conditionally decode arguments 4 and 5
based on IORING_ENTER_EXT_ARG and IORING_ENTER_EXT_ARG_REG flags.
When IORING_ENTER_EXT_ARG is set, decode as io_uring_getevents_arg
structure.  When IORING_ENTER_EXT_ARG_REG is set, print the byte
offset value.  When neither flag is set or both are set (invalid
case), use traditional sigset decoding for backward compatibility.

* Fix SIPS dialog downgrade via unvalidated target refresh (GHSA-vcvv-w84c-pfqq)

A secure dialog's target refresh (in-dialog request, or non-2xx/2xx
response to a dialog-creating request) applied the incoming Contact
URI to dlg->target without checking its scheme against dlg->secure.
Since dlg->target becomes the Request-URI of subsequent in-dialog
requests, and pjsip_get_dest_info()'s automatic-secure-transport
logic checks that same URI, a single non-SIPS Contact permanently
downgraded the dialog to plaintext.

Add dlg_target_refresh_allowed() and gate all three target-refresh
sites in sip_dialog.c on it: a secure dialog now ignores a non-SIPS
Contact instead of applying it.

Add dlg_target_refresh_test.c covering: malicious sip: Contact on a
secure dialog is ignored, legitimate sips: Contact on a secure
dialog still refreshes, and sip: Contact on a non-secure dialog
still refreshes (no regression).

Merge commit from fork

* pjlib-util: validate DNS responses against forgery

The asynchronous resolver matched responses to pending queries using only the
transaction ID, which was assigned sequentially, and did not check the response
source address or question section. This let an off-path attacker inject forged
responses (DNS cache poisoning), which in a SIP stack can redirect signaling.

- Accept a response only if it originates from a configured nameserver
  (matching address and port). Enabled by default; can be disabled per resolver
  via pj_dns_settings.disable_response_src_check /
  PJ_DNS_RESOLVER_DISABLE_RESPONSE_SRC_CHECK (a zero-initialized settings struct
  keeps the check enabled).
- Require the response question (name, type, and IN class) to match the
  outstanding query.
- Generate unpredictable transaction IDs as a truncated HMAC-SHA1 over a counter
  under a per-resolver secret key, so observed IDs do not reveal the generator
  state.

[pjsua] fix buffer overflow when call media count exceeds PJSUA_MAX_CALL_MEDIA (#5114)

* pjsua: fix buffer overflow when call media count exceeds PJSUA_MAX_CALL_MEDIA

An application-supplied aud_cnt/vid_cnt/txt_cnt larger than
PJSUA_MAX_CALL_MEDIA overran the fixed-size media index arrays in
pjsua_media_channel_init() and crashed the process.

apply_call_setting() now rejects such settings with PJ_ETOOMANY (now
also propagated by pjsua_call_answer2()), and pjsua_media_channel_init()
guards the arrays defensively as a safety net.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* pjsua: reject re-INVITE/UPDATE that would overflow call media arrays

The overflow fix in ece828963 guards apply_call_setting() and the initial
media branch, but a re-INVITE/UPDATE on an established call takes the
reinit branch of pjsua_media_channel_init(). That branch keeps every
existing (possibly disabled) m-line and only appends the newly requested
media, so the resulting media count can exceed P

* pjlib: fix buffer alignment in pj_pool_create_on_buf

The alignment adjustment added the misalignment amount to the buffer
pointer instead of the padding needed to reach the next boundary
(ALIGNMENT - misalignment). As a result the buffer -- and therefore the
pj_pool_t and first pj_pool_block placed at its start -- could remain
unaligned, risking unaligned access / SIGBUS on strict-alignment CPUs.
Compute the correct pad.

pjmedia/conference: fix races in synchronous removal of new ports (#5057)

pjmedia_conf_remove_port() removes a newly added port (whose ADD op is
still queued) synchronously: it cancels the port's pending ops under
the mutex, then releases the mutex and runs op_remove_port() and
op_remove_port2() on the calling thread.

This had two problems:

1. The port was not marked as "removing" before the mutex was
   released. Until op_remove_port2() frees the slot, the port still
   looks fully valid to other threads, so during the teardown window:

   - pjmedia_conf_connect_port() could queue a connect op on the dying
     slot. The clock thread could execute it during the teardown,
     adding a listener entry that points to a slot which is freed
     moments later. The next get_frame() tick then dereferences
     conf->ports[slot] == NULL and crashes.

   - a concurrent pjmedia_conf_remove_port() on the same port no
     longer finds the (already cancelled) ADD op and thus queues a
     REMO

Respond to RFC 5626 CRLF keep-alive ping on TCP and TLS transports (#5059)

* Respond to RFC 5626 CRLF keep-alive ping on TCP and TLS transports

pjsip only implements the sending side of the RFC 5626 (Section 4.4.1)
CRLF keep-alive: an idle connection periodically sends a double-CRLF
"ping" ("\r\n\r\n"). It never answered an incoming ping, so a peer that
uses CRLF keep-alives to probe liveness would see no "pong" and could
tear down or reconnect the flow.

Add the receiving side. When a stream transport (TCP or TLS) receives a
double CRLF at the start of the buffer, respond with a single CRLF
("\r\n") pong before handing the data to the parser, and consume the
ping byte(s). Detection is intentionally limited to the front of the
buffer: the receive buffer always begins at a SIP message boundary (whole
messages are consumed, partial messages keep their start-line at the
front), so a double CRLF appearing as message body or a header/body
separator is never mistaken for a ping.

* Don't fail ICE immediately when all checks complete without a valid pair (#4978)

When all of an agent's own connectivity checks complete without producing a
valid pair, ICE is declared failed immediately. This is premature when the
checks could not even be sent (e.g. the local routing or firewall rejects the
remote candidate address, failing the send with EPERM): the remote agent may
still be able to reach us and trigger a valid pair via an incoming check and
peer-reflexive candidate discovery. By failing and setting is_complete right
away, such incoming checks are dropped ("Ignored incoming check after ICE nego
has been completed").

Add a bounded grace window before declaring failure. When all checks have
completed with no valid pair, arm a TIMER_WAIT_VALID_PAIR timer (instead of
failing) and keep the session open so incoming checks can still form a valid
pair. If the timer expires first, ICE

Add on_uac_tsx_terminate_session callback for in-dialog 408/481 (#5000)

* Add on_uac_tsx_terminate_session callback for in-dialog 408/481

By RFC 3261 #12.2.1.2, an in-dialog UAC transaction that fails with 408
Request Timeout or 481 Call/Transaction Does Not Exist causes the
invite usage to be torn down via BYE. RFC 5057 #5.2 noted that this
rule should have been scoped to the invite usage, and some profiles
(e.g. ETSI EN 16072 eCall) require that only the operator may tear
down the call. The existing endpt.keep_inv_after_tsx_timeout flag is
global, binary, and only covers 408 -- not 481 -- so it cannot
discriminate by method or per call.

Add a new on_uac_tsx_terminate_session callback to pjsip_inv_callback
that fires inside handle_uac_tsx_response() and inv_handle_update_response()
just before BYE/end-session, letting the application return PJ_TRUE to
keep the session alive. Bridge it through pjsua_callback as
on_call_tsx_terminate_session, and through pjsua2 as
Call::onCallTsxTerm

Account-scoped server affinity: UDP destination-pinning (#4964) (#4977)

* pjsua: server affinity (#4964) — UDP destination-pinning via hidden Route

Pin UDP destination by injecting "<sip:host;lr;hide>" at the head of
acc->route_set. The ;hide URI param suppresses the Route from the
wire (handled in pjsip_routing_hdr_print) but loose-routing still uses
it as the request destination — so REGISTER/INVITE go to the pinned
address even though the listener is shared. TCP/TLS already pin via
the transport selector; this closes the UDP gap for the same feature.

A single sa_sync_route_set() handles both apply and push: it adds or
removes the hidden Route from acc->route_set based on the current pin
state, then forwards to regc only if the diff against sa_pushed_route
(mirror of last push) is non-empty. update_hdr_list does the diff,
which avoids the per-call regc->pool clone that
pjsip_regc_set_route_set does unconditionally.

destroy_regc resets sa_pushed_route so the next push after a regc

x86-64: fix mixed-class struct varargs in the runtime helpers

Two SysV AMD64 bugs corrupted a {double,long}-style (SSE+INTEGER) struct
passed as a vararg, so every such struct after the first read a stale or
overlapping SSE slot:

  * _MIR_get_ff_call over-counted SSE registers for block arguments: an
    all-INTEGER block bumped n_xregs by its qwords, and the mixed
    INTEGER+SSE / SSE+INTEGER cases bumped n_xregs around the single SSE
    eightbyte (copy-pasted from the Win64 path, where integer and vector
    slots advance in lockstep).  The callee read the SSE half one XMM
    register too high through the interpreter FFI.

  * va_block_arg_builtin advanced fp_offset by 8 after an SSE eightbyte,
    but SSE slots in the register save area are 16 bytes apart (matching
    the SSE-only case and va_arg_builtin); the next mixed struct read an
    overlapping slot.  Used by both the interpreter and generated code.

Fixes gcc.c-torture/execute/stdarg-3.c under c2m -ei.

Fixes #456.

Take the slow out-of-SSA path for self-predecessor blocks (lost copy)

make_conventional_ssa's same-bb fast path renamed a phi result and all
its uses to the congruence-class register.  When the phi's block is its
own predecessor, the back-edge phi-input copy is inserted at the end of
that same block, before the tail branch -- so a renamed use in the
branch read the next iteration's value (the classic lost-copy problem).
A `while (i-- > 0)` loop whose condition tests the phi var directly ran
one iteration short.

Take the slow path (mov var, dest_var after the phi; uses keep var)
whenever the block is a self-predecessor.

Fixes gcc.c-torture/execute/pr43236.c under the generator.

Fixes #454.

c2mir: fix two statement-expression value bugs

1. A struct/union statement-expression value reused a stack slot.
   `({ ...; obj; })` whose value is a struct/union returns the lvalue of
   an in-block local, but c2mir reused that local's stack slot across
   non-overlapping sibling scopes, so two such statement-expressions in
   one expression both read whichever block ran last.  Copy the aggregate
   result into a fresh ALLOCA temporary (the mechanism complex_temp uses)
   so each value has independent storage.  Fixes
   gcc.c-torture/execute/20020320-1.c.

2. A statement-expression ending in x++/x-- left an undef operand.
   Expression-statements are gen'd value-discarded, but post-inc/dec only
   materialize their old value in value context, so `({ x--; })` used as a
   value or condition produced an undef operand and crashed codegen.  Gen
   the block's last expression in value context.  Fixes
   gcc.c-torture/execute/950906-1.c.

Fixes #452.

c2mir: give storage to a struct/union va_arg used as an rvalue

A struct/union va_arg with no destination object -- used directly as an
rvalue, e.g. `va_arg(ap, struct S).m` -- hit an unfinished path that
moved 0 into the result register and used it as the va_block_arg
destination, so the aggregate was written to address 0 (NULL) and read
back from a bogus base: a miscompile / SIGSEGV.

Allocate a frame temporary for the aggregate and present it as the
result lvalue, mirroring the desirable-dest path.  (The buffer is an
alloca, so a struct va_arg rvalue inside a loop grows the frame -- a
reserved frame slot would avoid that; correct either way.)

Fixes the C reproducer in #441.

Fix x86-64 va_start offsets for functions with block args

va_start machinization re-derived the named args' register/stack layout
with its own scan instead of using the state the prologue walk just
computed, and the scan disagreed with the actual layout in three ways:

  * register-passed blocks (BLK+1/BLK+2/...) were not counted into
    gp_offset/fp_offset, so va_arg read the named structs' registers
    from the save area as if they were varargs;
  * every block was added to the overflow-area displacement, including
    ones actually passed in registers, and without the 8-byte rounding
    the argument area applies, so stack varargs were read from wrong
    offsets;
  * fp_offset exhaustion checked gp_offset >= 176.

Replace the scan with the int_arg_num/fp_arg_num/mem_size totals left
by the prologue arg walk (what the aarch64 port already does), which
agree with the layout by construction.

aarch64: do not clobber x9 in the bb thunk's branch to the bb wrapper

_MIR_get_bb_thunk emits 'x9 = bb_version' followed by a branch to the
bb wrapper, emitted via _MIR_redirect_thunk.  The redirect's far form
is 'ldr x9, 8; br x9', which overwrites x9 -- the register carrying
bb_version -- with the wrapper's own address.  Whenever a bb thunk is
published farther than a direct branch can reach (+-128MB) from the
wrapper, the wrapper passes its own address as the bb_version to
bb_version_generator, which then reads machine code bytes as a struct
bb_version: garbage attrs typically grow spot2attr toward tens of GB
(OOM), or crash.

Seen as a deterministic OOM of c2mir-bb-bootstrap-test on musl libc
(aarch64): mallocng's mmap-heavy allocation pattern interleaves with
the code holder mappings and pushes them out of direct-branch range of
the early-allocated wrapper.  glibc's brk-based heap keeps code
holders clustered, hiding the bug at bootstrap scale; any sufficiently
large -eb workload

Fix long double stack alignment in aarch64 va_arg_builtin and ff interface

Two places rounding up to 16 used "% 16" instead of "/ 16 * 16":
va_arg_builtin replaced va->__stack with a value in 0..15 (crashing on
the first binary128 long double vararg taken from the stack), and
_MIR_get_ff_call computed a wrong stack offset for long double args
past the 8 v-registers, corrupting the 9th+ FP argument.

Fix IBL specular/diffuse artifacts: two-step panorama→cubemap pipeline

Instead of sampling the equirectangular panorama directly in the specular
and diffuse prefilter shaders, first convert the panorama to a mipmapped
GL_TEXTURE_CUBE_MAP (512×512, full mip chain), then filter from that
cubemap. This matches the architecture of the glTF Sample Viewer and
eliminates the firefly/sparkle artifacts caused by the non-uniform texel
density of the equirectangular projection.

Changes:
- glus_ibl.c: add iblMipLevels() helper and buildSourceCubemap() internal
  function; glusIblBuildSpecularEnvironmentMap and
  glusIblBuildDiffuseEnvironmentMap now build the intermediate cubemap
  first and pass it (+ u_width) to their respective shaders
- glus_ibl_specular.frag.glsl: use samplerCube u_cubemapTexture and
  u_width; update LOD formula to 0.5*log2(6*W²/(N*pdf)) matching the
  glTF Sample Viewer; drop panorama() UV helper
- glus_ibl_diffuse.frag.glsl: same cubemap sampler + u_width; add
  per-samp

Add Example47: GPU 3D spatial colour sort via subgroup shuffle

Novel odd-even transposition sort on a 3D RGBA8 image3D.
N^3 unique RGB8 lattice colours are shuffled randomly then sorted
along X (by R), Y (by G) and Z (by B) axes until convergence to
the RGB cube where texel(x,y,z).rgb = (x,y,z)*255/(N-1).

Highlights:
- OpenGL 4.6 / GLSL 460 compute shader
- GL_KHR_shader_subgroup_shuffle: no shared memory, no barriers
- GRID_N queried from GL_SUBGROUP_SIZE_KHR at runtime
- Animated step by step so the crystallisation is visible

Controls:
  Space  - start sort animation
  F      - finish all remaining steps instantly
  + / -  - increase / decrease per-step delay (default 100 ms)
  R      - reshuffle and restart

Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>

column6:
Re-seed server global packet sequence on start, not just create

Global packets (connection challenge, connection denied) encrypt with
the same per-connect-token server-to-client key as per-client packets,
whose sequences start at zero. The global sequence therefore starts at
1ULL << 63 so the AEAD nonces stay disjoint under the shared key.

That seed was only applied in netcode_server_create, and
netcode_server_stop reset the global sequence to zero. A server that
was stopped and started again sent challenge packets from global
sequence 0, 1, 2 ... overlapping the per-client sequence space: the
same key and nonce encrypting two different plaintexts, which breaks
the AEAD security guarantees.

Seed the global sequence in netcode_server_start as well. No wire
format change. Pinned by test_server_restart_global_sequence.

Found while porting netcode to Rust (mas-bandwidth/netcode.rs).

Add netcode_server_create_error, distinguishing bind failures

The server-side mirror of netcode_client_create_error: each failure path
in server create records a NETCODE_SERVER_CREATE_ERROR_* code, queryable
via netcode_server_create_error() when create returns NULL.

Bind failures are reported separately from other socket errors, per
address family: a port already in use is the common operational failure
for dedicated servers, and callers want to react to it (try the next
port) differently than to a socket that could not be created at all.

With this, create failures are queryable on both client and server. The
running server intentionally has no state machine beyond
netcode_server_running: its only states are stopped and started, and
everything else is per-client.

Adds test_server_create_error covering every reachable code, including
real port-in-use bind collisions for both address families. Suite is now
42 tests.

Reference count netcode_init, default zeroed configs, deterministic simulator rng

Three ergonomics and reproducibility fixes:

- netcode_init/netcode_term are reference counted, so multiple subsystems
  in the same application can init and term independently. Previously a
  second init was assert-only and silently re-ran platform init in release.

- netcode_client_create/netcode_server_create default the allocator
  functions if the caller passes a zeroed config instead of calling
  netcode_default_*_config first. Previously this was a NULL deref.

- The network simulator uses a per-instance seeded xorshift64* instead of
  global rand(). Simulator behavior is now deterministic across runs and
  isolated from application use of rand(). netcode_random_float is removed;
  it was only used by the simulator.

Adds test_init_and_defaults and test_network_simulator_determinism
(suite is now 40 tests).

Fix timing-sensitive real-socket connect tests exposed by CI

client_server_socket_connect_to advances virtual time in a busy loop while
pumping real sockets, so virtual timeouts (connect token expiry, connection
request timeout) could expire before the OS delivered a single loopback
packet. Failed on the macOS Release CI runner. Sleep 10ms per iteration so
real packet delivery keeps pace with virtual time.

Also in this commit (small API hardening):

- netcode_parse_address: ports are now validated (all digits, <= 65535)
  instead of silently truncating through atoi + uint16_t cast. New tests.
- netcode_client_send_packet / netcode_server_send_packet reject zero-byte
  payloads with an error log. The receiver already dropped them on the wire,
  so previously they silently vanished.

Fix bugs found in code review: IPv6 address parsing, Linux packet tagging, and more

- netcode_parse_address: bracketed IPv6 addresses with 1-2 digit ports
  (e.g. "[::1]:5") failed to parse, and short addresses like "[fe80::1]:5"
  were corrupted mid-parse. The port scan now breaks once the port colon
  is found, and requires it to be preceded by ']'. Bracketed addresses
  without a port ("[::1]") now parse with port 0, matching unbracketed
  behavior.

- Packet tagging was silently dead code on Linux: the guard referenced
  NETCODE_PLATFORM_LINUX which is never defined (evaluates to 0), and the
  body referenced socket->handle where the parameter is named s. Now
  guarded by NETCODE_PLATFORM_UNIX with the correct handle.

- Failed socket() calls were not detected on Mac/Unix: the handle is an
  unsigned size_t, so -1 wraps and "<= 0" never matched. Now checks for
  (netcode_socket_handle_t) -1 explicitly.

- netcode_client_send_packet / netcode_server_send_packet enforced the
  max p

[airplay] Reassemble event messages that arrive in several reads

A HomePod's Siri "stop"/"play" arrives on the AirPlay event channel as a
POST /command with a ~965 byte binary plist body, which the HomePod sends in
two TCP segments (observed: 920 + 45 bytes). rtsp_parse() parsed each read on
its own, so the first failed with "Could not parse incoming event plist", the
second with "no plist body found", incoming_cb() drained the buffer after
each, and the command never reached handle_event().

incoming_cb() already has a "return 1 = wait for more data" path; make
rtsp_parse() use it by checking the message's Content-Length before trying
to parse the body. Oversized buffers (>64 KiB) are discarded so a
never-completing message can't grow the pending buffer without bound.

Tested with OwnTone 29.3 on a Raspberry Pi 3 and a HomePod ("Living Room"):
before the change Siri stop was ignored; after it the log shows "Incomplete
AirPlay event (1024 bytes so far), waiting for more data" followed

WT-15324 Decode UTF-8 without iconv in test/model (#14443)

## Summary

- `decode_utf8()` converted UTF-8 to `WCHAR_T` via `iconv`. That path
goes through the C library's character conversion routines, which are
locale-dependent and, on macOS, **silently drop NUL code points** —
`iconv` consumes all input, reports success, and emits one fewer wide
char.
- A metadata key such as `file:WiredTigerHS.wt\0` therefore lost its
terminator. Unpacking it with format `"S"` then failed
`WT_SIZE_CHECK_UNPACK` in `__wt_struct_unpack` (needs `strlen+1 = 21`,
has `maxlen = 20`) with `EINVAL`, so every test/model binary aborted
with `Failed to unpack data_value`.
- Under the default C locale the same conversion also rejected any code
point above U+007F with `EILSEQ` — which is the primary documented use
case of `decode_utf8`, recovering packed integer keys (WiredTiger packs
key `1` as byte `0x81`). `setlocale()` fixes that one but **not** the
NUL drop.
- Decode UTF-8 by hand instead. Only code points

WT-18156 Keep untimestamped snapshot reads consistent across follower checkpoint pickups (#14363)

On a disaggregated follower, a layered cursor binds its stable
constituent at first use to the newest adopted checkpoint. Adopted
content has its transaction ids wiped, so a transaction at snapshot
isolation without a read timestamp cannot exclude it: a bind to a
checkpoint adopted after the snapshot silently exposes post-snapshot
data — torn transactions, non-repeatable reads, vanishing keys, and new
tables leaking wholesale.

This change makes such transactions observe exactly their snapshot, with
checkpoint pickups never refusing a reader.

WT-18190 (#14360) has merged, so this change now sits directly on
develop. It defines, sets and reads no statistic: the observability for
it is stacked on top in WT-18251.

### The change

- Every untimestamped snapshot records, at establishment, the checkpoint
it covers and the role era it belongs to, with a validate-and-retry
making establishment

static WT_INLINE void
__txn_snapshot_record_disagg(WT_SESSION_IMPL *session)
{
    WT_CONNECTION_IMPL *conn = S2C(session);

    /*
     * Enter the role-change generation: the published generation is the snapshot's recorded role
     * era, compared at every stable bind. Both generations entered here are left wherever the
     * snapshot's era ends: a failed validation, a snapshot refresh, or the snapshot's release.
     */
    __wt_session_gen_enter(session, WT_GEN_DISAGG_ROLE);
    /*
     * Acquire-read the role: it is published with a release store after the role-change generation
     * is bumped, so a snapshot that records the new role also observes the new generation and
     * cannot validate against the era it just left.
     */
    session->txn->disagg_role_leader =
      __wt_atomic_load_bool_acquire(&conn->layered_table_manager.leader);

    /*
     * Only a follower pins a checkpoint: its stable binds compare against the pin. A leader's
     * stable table is written with local transaction ids and needs no pin, and its own checkpoints
     * advance the checkpoint generation, so pinning would rebuild every snapshot that overlaps a
     * checkpoint completion. A snapshot from before a step-down is left unpinned and refused if it
     * binds checkpoint content afterwards.
     *
     * The checkpoint generation is the newest checkpoint delivered plus one, advanced when the
     * metadata arrives, even before its adoption completes: arrival implies its content is already
     * replayed into the ingest tables, so this snapshot covers it. Until the adoption completes,
     * the pin is simply newer than anything the stable can bind, which is always safe.
     *
     * Entering the generation publishes the pin with the manager's full-barrier recheck, pairing
     * with a delivery's generation advance: a delivery either observes the pin published here, or
     * the validation after the build observes the delivery and retries.
     */
    if (!session->txn->disagg_role_leader)
        __wt_session_gen_enter(session, WT_GEN_DISAGG_CKPT);
}

WT-18190 Unroll the checkpoint pickup's metadata merge on failure (#14360)

The checkpoint pickup applied its local metadata updates one autocommit
at a time — the checkpoint entry, then one merge per layered table —
with no compensation path. A failure partway left a partially adopted
checkpoint: tables already merged resolved to the new checkpoint while
the published LSN still admitted only the old one, so a stable cursor
bound in that window could read content its transaction snapshot cannot
exclude. The only recovery was to panic and let the restarted node
discard its local state, which also made a transient conflict with a
concurrent metadata writer — replicated DDL, for instance — fatal.

The merge now runs under metadata tracking, so a failure unrolls every
update already made, including any ingest tables created along the way,
and the node stays on its previous checkpoint. A write conflict becomes
a clean retryable failure, reported as `EBUSY`. Ingest table creation is
hoisted

WT-18077 Rework __wt_verify checkpoint error handling (#14209)

## Summary
- Extract the per-checkpoint work in `__wt_verify` into a new
`__verify_one_checkpoint` helper so the checkpoint is always unloaded
via a cleanup label, fixing a leak where `WT_ERR` from
`__wti_btree_tree_open` / the root dump message / the diagnostic size
check jumped past `checkpoint_unload` (and, in the size-check case, left
the `evict_disabled` refcount unbalanced).
- Move the eviction re-acquire + tree discard into the cleanup label
under an `evict_off` guard, so every post-load exit path re-acquires the
exclusive lock (mandatory refcount balance) and discards the tree before
unloading the checkpoint.
- Add `WT_ERR(ret)` after `__verify_tree` to bail immediately on a hard
failure; this is a no-op in `read_corrupt` mode (where the error is
stashed in `vs->verify_err`), so the remaining checks still run.
- Keep `WT_TRET`/`WT_TRET_MSG` for the accumulate-size, page-discard,
history-store, and cleanup calls: ev

Equalizer3Bands: template on arithmetic type for FPU-less MCUs

Equalizer3BandsT<T>/Equalizer3BandsPerChannelT<T> generalize the 3-band
equalizer's internal filter state/coefficients from a hard-coded float to
an arbitrary numeric type, so q1_14_t or soft_float_t can be used on boards
like the RP2040 to avoid software-emulated float instructions. float-based
Equalizer3Bands/Equalizer3BandsPerChannel remain as backwards-compatible
aliases; verified bit-identical hot-path codegen for T=float and added
tests-cmake/equalizer covering float/q1_14_t/soft_float_t behavior.

v1.1.1: Fix safety bugs, add user_data callback context, improve docs

Bug fixes:
- Fix linked list corruption when button_stop() called from callback
  by caching next pointer before invoking handler in button_ticks()
- Fix ticks counter overflow: saturate at UINT16_MAX instead of wrapping
- Execute callbacks outside the lock to prevent deadlock (no recursive
  mutex needed)

Feature: add void* user_data context pointer to callbacks (breaking API
change - BtnCallback now takes (Button*, void*), button_attach() takes
an extra void* user_data parameter)

Tests: add 6 new tests (stop-in-callback safety, ticks saturation,
triple click, user_data delivery, debounce boundary, rapid stress test)

Docs: rewrite both READMEs with state machine detail, FAQ, callback
context notes, LONG_PRESS_HOLD throttling guidance, migration guide

glm: the format it needed, the channel it always opens, and the branch nobody had verified

Four things stood between "converted and answers a question" and "usable".
Two were a chat format nobody had written down, one was a verification, and
one was a measurement that killed the work it was meant to justify.

chat.json gained prelude, think and stop, and each exists because GLM's
format cannot be written without it: it opens every conversation with
[gMASK]<sop>, which belongs to no role; its turns end when the *next* role
marker begins rather than with a suffix; and its generation prompt always
opens a reasoning channel the model closes itself. Written without `stop`
the format answers correctly and then runs on into the next turn, answering
questions nobody asked — the container's eos_token_id is <|endoftext|>,
which is right for a raw continuation and is not what ends a chat turn.
Both Kimi formats are unchanged: stop defaults to the assistant suffix.

serve/chatfmt.py said a chat.j

ram: take the machine the user has, and let residency pick the schedule

The automatic budget walked a ladder whose top rung was floor + 3x a
token's working set. That is what recommended_bytes means — worth having,
without knowing the machine — and it is the wrong ceiling once the machine
is known: on this 64 GB laptop Kimi-Linear's entire 17.17 GB expert set
fits and the default gave it 1.65 GB of cache.

The real ceiling is the container's own bank, published now as
plan.bank_bytes: a cache that holds every expert never reads one twice, and
a byte past that is a slot nothing will ever fill. The ladder starts there
and walks down, capped at the bank. `waste plan` calls that budget fully
resident. Nothing about §39's and §56's cliff changes — the cap that guards
it is still three quarters of what the process may use — and an unfilled
slot is address space, not memory.

Two things followed that were not the plan.

glm: GLM-5.3-Flash, and the three things it adds to this engine

zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash — 313 B parameters, 328 GB of fp8, published
yesterday — turned out to be mostly this engine already. The layer mix
(34 KDA, 11 MLA), the KDA parameterization, the absorbed MLA, the
sigmoid/top-k router, the fp8 reader and the nested text_config with a
language_model. prefix are all K3's, and qk_rope_head_dim 0 together with
mla_use_nope means the rotary is not reached at all.

Three things are new, each behind a config key absent everywhere else:

  mHC          four parallel residual streams instead of one, collapsed
               into each sublayer by learned weights and scattered back
               through a Sinkhorn-projected doubly-stochastic matrix.
  clamped      gate above, up on both sides, before the SiLU. The
  SwiGLU       family's three activations are now waste_act_pair_range
               rather than an if/else at seven call sites.
  DSA k-pool   an MLA layer scores pools of four c

yesterday — turned out to be mostly this engine already. The layer mix
(34 KDA, 11 MLA), the KDA parameterization, the absorbed MLA, the
sigmoid/top-k router, the fp8 reader and the nested text_config with a
language_model. prefix are all K3's, and qk_rope_head_dim 0 together with
mla_use_nope means the rotary is not reached at all.

Three things are new, each behind a config key absent everywhere else:

  mHC          four parallel residual streams instead of one, collapsed
               into each sublayer by learned weights and scattered back
               through a Sinkhorn-projected doubly-stochastic matrix.
  clamped      gate above, up on both sides, before the SiLU. The
  SwiGLU       family's three activations are now waste_act_pair_range
               rather than an if/else at seven call sites.
  DSA k-pool   an MLA layer scores pools of four c

exp1: a thread pool that knows which cores are fast, on by default

LEARNED §47 named this and declined to build it: 'a pool that knows which
cores are performance cores and sizes SIMD-heavy work to them while
leaving the latency-bound kernels the whole machine.' Three kernels on
this branch wanted it.

waste_perf_cpu_count() answers 6 here from hw.perflevel0.logicalcpu, the
big.LITTLE cpu_capacity reading on Linux, and 0 where the question has no
answer — which makes the whole thing a no-op on a uniform machine. The
pool's fast group is the calling thread plus workers 0..n_fast-2, created
at QOS_CLASS_USER_INTERACTIVE because macOS has no affinity API and the
class is the entire mechanism. waste_parallel_for_fast() cuts work for
that group; WASTE_WIDE selects which call sites use it.

The first version measured exactly nothing — 1.181 against 1.182 tok/s.

exp1: the VQ3R apply through a register-held int8 table

WASTE_VQ8=1 puts the VQ3R gather through vqtbl4q against an int8 shadow of
the table instead of walking a 1.34 MB fp32 one. vqtbl4q answers 0 past
index 63, so a 256-entry table is four lookups over c, c-64, c-128, c-192
added together with no select; vld3q_u8 deinterleaves the [row][stage]
index layout sixteen rows at a time, which is what makes a stage-major
loop affordable. §41 measured this shape at 1.24x and stopped; it is 1.76x
here.

1.76x on the kernel, 1.19x on the bucket, 1.05x end to end — and that gap
is §46's unexplained scaling failure reproduced by a third kernel. At six
threads the same comparison is 1.32x and the run is 24% slower overall,
because the trunk matvec loses 60 -> 32 GB/s without the E-cores. Neither
thread count is right for both. §47's parked recommendation — a pool that
knows which cores are performance cores — now has three kernels behind it.

says the most accurate kernel is the second worst. On K3 a teacher-forced
logit norm over more than a few tokens measures when the router first
flips an expert, not how much arithmetic moved:

exp1: trunk-matvec profile bucket, a faster Q4G kernel, and the Metal gate re-run

The dense trunk matvec had no bucket in WASTE_PROFILE, so 28.5 GB of Q4G
per token — three quarters of what a K3 decode step reads — was being
counted inside 'kda'. It is 46% of a top-8 step and the largest single
item in it.

- P_TMV: matvec_t is timed, counted and reported in bytes and GB/s.
- waste_mvq_rows_f32 unpacks Q4G nibbles in registers instead of staging
  them through a byte buffer: 1.24x on the kernel, bit-identical logits
  (cmp-clean against the previous build on a real container).
- WASTE_SDOT4 puts the Q4G trunk through SDOT with deinterleaved int8
  activations. 1.22x end to end and off by default: on K3 it measures
  KL 0.289 teacher-forced, past every bar this repo applies.

  arm, sdot4= and devkb= arms, WASTE_SWEEP_TOPK, WASTE_SWEEP_IDS.

  loa

Let a host say which CPUs the pool runs on, and refuse when it cannot

Third-party measurement, issue #23: on a Ryzen 9 9900X — Zen 5, two 6-core
CCDs with separate 32 MB L3 — six threads on one CCD ran Kimi-Linear-48B
16-25% faster than the same six split across both, at byte-identical work
(bytes_read 15244357632 and the same hit counts in every arm). Giving those
six threads all 24 CPUs to migrate between costs a further ~10%. The other
CCD alone reproduces the single-die number to 0.5%, and the penalty is
unchanged under WASTE_XPAR=1 (-24.9% against -25.0%), so it is a property of
where the threads run rather than of how the work is cut.

The engine had no way to say. waste_cfg.cpu_list does now, with --cpus LIST
on the CLI and on `python3 -m serve`, and WASTE_CPUS in the environment.
Linux binds with sched_setaffinity, Windows with SetThreadAffinityMask.

the fast cores — as a 25% gain on Kimi-Linear and a 3

Add WQ_VQ4P, and measure what the table-lookup kernel is actually worth

A 256-entry VQ stage table is sixteen vector registers on a machine with
thirty-two, which is the whole reason the VQ3R gather stayed scalar however
§25 unrolled it. WQ_VQ4P spends the same 24 bits per 8-dim vector as four
6-bit indices into 64-entry tables instead of three 8-bit ones: same 3.00
bits/weight, same record size, and a stage table that is one vqtbl4q.

The kernel delivers. In isolation it is 3.88x, and that survives a
gigabyte of index stream, so it is not a cache artefact — tools/lutbw.c
exists to re-check that in a minute. In the engine it is 1.18x on
Kimi-Linear and 1.09x on K3, both measured with each container on the same
storage as its baseline. The gap between 3.88x on a bench and 1.17x in
place is the finding, and it is not explained: VQ4P runs at its
single-thread rate inside the pool (25.3 -> 27.2 GB/s across ten threads)
while VQ3R scales 3.6x. Not the chunk size, not memory bandwidth. §46

Size the automatic budget against the cgroup limit, not the host's RAM

The resolver had one machine number in it and on Linux it was the wrong
one. waste_physical_ram() is sysconf(_SC_PHYS_PAGES) there, which reports
the host's MemTotal and reports exactly the same thing from inside a
cgroup allowed a fraction of it. Every containerized run has therefore
been sizing against RAM it was never going to get: K3 in a 32 GiB cgroup
on a 256 GiB host resolves floor + 3x, asks for about 80 GB, and is
killed.

This is not §16 and does not behave like it. That cliff is a performance
failure with a shape — hit rate climbs, bytes read fall, throughput drops
eightfold, and a sweep finds it. A cgroup limit is a kill: nothing
degrades first and no cache policy softens it. It is the same class of
bug as §27, a platform path every green run had avoided rather than
exercised.

the 7/8 reserve, the whole-working-set stepping, the

Built from §34's measurement. At the end of moe_layer, once this layer's
sixteen reads are consumed and the disk is about to idle through the next

§30 measured mlock on the expert cache and called it a reproducibility win.
The comparison was incomplete — a wired cache against nothing, both on a
worked machine, never asking whether the other buffer was the one to pin.

straight after a 58 GiB row had driven the machine into paging:

  trunk only  0.57         |  0.56-0.57

is the mechanism §30 hypothesized now measured rather than argued: pinning
17.5 GB of a cache that hits 19% leaves the 27.5 GB trunk, read in full
every token, as the pageable part. Wiring the trunk is the best in every
single run, and wiring both adds nothing over the trunk alone.

Linux asked for 16 KiB alignment where O_DIRECT wanted 4

Fixes #4, reported by Kevin McCoy. bank_open gated the bypass on
WASTE_DIO_ALIGN (16384, the buffer alignment Metal needs) where O_DIRECT
constrains offset and length, which the format guarantees in WASTE_ALIGN
units of 4096. No container has ever passed that test, so Linux opened
every expert bank buffered while reporting "direct_io": false.

The constant alone is not enough: O_DIRECT accepts the open and fails
every transfer the device dislikes, so bank_probe now reads one block at
offset 0 and the descriptor is kept only if that succeeds.

Verified in a Debian container on 6.12: direct_io false -> true, the
WASTE_DIRECT=0 veto intact, the fallback exercised by forcing the probe
to fail, and gcc's warning count unchanged at 19. macOS unaffected and
still 38/38.

LEARNED §16's cliff is not the cache missing, it is a cache hit turning
into a page fault: the engine stays inside its budget, the machine does
not, and 29 GB of cache runs eight times slower than 17. Purgeable memory
is the shape of an answer — under pressure the kernel discards a volatile
object outright instead of compressing and swapping it, and a discarded
slot is just a miss, which is the pread the engine already does.

pread by blocking pread, with the arithmetic waiting on each — even
though every id is known before the first read.

Fourteen defects, mostly in what happens when a second thread — or a
second context — exists at all.

a mutex now, none of them on a hot path — cpu_features runs at load.

Sample in one pass, or in a sort — not in a quadratic scan

waste_gen_params.top_k defaults to 0, and sample() read that as "no
limit" by setting k = vocab. The selection sort under it then ran over
the whole vocabulary for every one of those k positions: on K3's 163840
entries that is 1.34e10 comparisons, measured at 27.9 seconds per token,
single threaded.

Nothing exotic reaches it. `waste run --temp 0.8` with no --top-k does,
and so does every OpenAI client that sets temperature, because top_k is
not a field OpenAI has — serve leaves it at 0 by construction.

The work the caller actually asked for decides the work done. With
neither top-k nor top-p there is nothing to truncate, so the full softmax
is the distribution and ranking it buys nothing: one pass, 0.6 ms. With
either, the candidates have to be ranked, and that is a sort rather than
a scan: 22.8 ms. Ties break by id so a seed reproduces a run whatever
qsort does with equal keys, and the RNG advances once per call on both

Bound the sequence to the context, and the four ways past the buffer

An expert record is checked on the way in and a manifest is bounded before
it sizes anything, but the numbers the engine computes for itself were
trusted. Four of them were wrong, all reproduced under ASan against a
synthetic container.

`mla_layer` writes one latent per position and nothing bounded the
position. `waste chat` accumulates across turns and `waste run` accepts a
prompt of MAXTOK against a --ctx of 4096, so both walked off the end of
latcache — quietly, with the answer still coming out. kv_cap is a real
bound now: refused at the public API before a prompt is evaluated, so the
conversation is left as it was, and a generation that reaches the ceiling
stops there and returns OK, which is the same kind of end as max_tokens.
waste_error_detail says which one it was, and the CLI prints it — silence
there reads as a model with nothing more to say.

m->att has four users and was sized for one. The router parks i

windows: build it, run it in CI, and the 32-bit long it was hiding

The previous commit measured what Windows would cost and pinned the
number: three POSIX calls with no equivalent, plus
FILE_FLAG_NO_BUFFERING for the bypass. That estimate was right about
the three calls and wrong about the size, because it counted what
fails to compile.

Two things that compile cleanly were the actual work.

`long` is 32 bits on Windows. LLP64 widens only pointers, so every
file offset in the engine was a silent 2 GB truncation on a format
whose small container is 17 GB and whose large one is 982 GB:
pread_all's argument, waste_tensor.file_off, the manifest's off and
scale_off through js_int, a bank's `bytes` before it is divided into
records. None of it is a compile error and none of it is visible on a
machine where long is 64 bits. They are int64_t now, which is a no-op
on macOS and Linux and the difference between reading the right expert
and the wrong one on Windows.

engine: read the release instead of deducing it

Six files in the K3 repo had never been downloaded, because the
downloader asked for a hardcoded list of names. Reading them corrected
four things the engine had inferred, and one it had got right.

**Image normalization was the CLIP convention.** K3 ships
preprocessor_config.json and it says mean = std = 0.5 — normalization to
[-1, 1], which kimi_k3_vision_processing.py applies from media_proc_cfg.
The CLIP means differ by up to 0.09 and the deviations by nearly 2x, so
every image the engine encoded reached the tower with the wrong contrast
and a colour cast. Nothing caught it: the tower's oracle runs on
torch.randn pixels and never calls the image loader, and test_image
checks (v - mean) / std against constants it defines itself.

**The media block was missing the resolution.** K3 wraps an image as
`<|media_begin|>image WxH<|media_content|><|media_pad|><|media_end|>`,
with the source dimensions as text — a fact the model was trained to

vision: prove the model sees the image, and price it honestly

A tower that matches its oracle to 2.3e-06 proves the arithmetic, not
that the embeddings mean anything where they land. So: one prompt,
"Caption: A photograph of a", run with and without an image, compared by
next-token distribution.

Control, no image — the model's prior over what photographs are of:

    man .081 | person .068 | woman .068 | young .039 | white .028

With a photograph of a rocky coastal mountain above dark water:

    rugged .156 | mountain .116 | rocky .106 | mountainous .099
    body .096 | large .067 | coastal .058 | lake .039

With an abstract render of glossy pale-blue tubes on white:

    white .081 | close .063 | single .036 | glass .029
    blurry .028 | metal .026 | blue .021 | clear .021

Every person word is gone in both, and each distribution describes its
own picture. The peak sharpens from .081 to .156, which is the model
being less uncertain because it has something to look at.

vision: images reach the public API and the command line

Three calls, not one: waste_image_add encodes and queues, and returns how
many positions the image will take; waste_image_expand rewrites one
placeholder into that many slots; generate consumes the queue. The split
exists because a host has to be able to size a prompt before committing
to it — an image is not a token, it is a few hundred of them, and finding
that out during prefill is too late.

Expand refuses a prompt whose placeholder count does not match the queue
rather than doing something reasonable-looking. A silent mismatch would
surface much later as an image the model never saw, which is a far worse
bug to chase than an error at the call site.

The queue is armed before prefill and released after, so a second turn
about the same picture does not splice it in again — the first turn's
positions are already in the attention state.

CLI: --image FILE, repeatable, which also switches cfg.vision on. The
tower is loaded only

vision: images in, embeddings spliced at the media placeholder

third_party/stb_image.h (v2.30, public domain) is the engine's one
vendored dependency, compiled into src/image.c and nowhere else. Decoding
PNG and JPEG by hand is a project of its own; a single header with no
build system, no configuration and no transitive dependencies is a
different proposition from a library.

src/image.c decodes, resizes to a whole number of 14-pixel patches with
an even count on both axes (the tower merges 2x2), normalizes, and lays
the result out channel-major as the conv kernel expects. Verified against
a solid-red PNG: the centre pixel comes out +1.9303 / -1.7521 / -1.4802,
which is exactly (1-mean)/std and (0-mean)/std per channel.

The splice is an expansion, not a substitution — that is what the
reference does. One <|media_pad|> (163605) in the prompt becomes N

Special tokens, and stop paying RAM for a vision tower we never read

Checking the engine against a hosted-API guide for K3 turned up two real
defects, neither of them in the guide's subject matter.

The tokenizer had no concept of special tokens. tiktoken's rank file
holds merges only; K3's markup — <|open|>, <|media_begin|>, [EOS] —
lives in tokenizer_config.json and was never converted, so <|open|>
tokenized as six ordinary tokens. That silently destroys any chat
template, which makes the chat-template work of the previous commit
useless on a real model, and would have destroyed the media markers an
image is wrapped in. The converter now writes specials.json; the
tokenizer matches those strings whole and longest-first before the
pre-tokenizer runs. Verified on K3: <|media_begin|> is 163602, <|open|>
is 163587, ordinary text is byte-identical.

never read — 223 MB, because every lookup goes through

make asan runs the suite under ASan/UBSan; make fuzz mutates containers;

io: bypass the page cache on Linux too, and unbreak the Linux build

ecache.h has always claimed reads bypass the page cache — the whole
hit-rate argument rests on it, since a 17 GB container on a 64 GB
machine would otherwise be measuring the kernel's cache. macOS did it
with fcntl(F_NOCACHE). Linux had the claim in a comment and nothing in
the code.

bank_open now opens with O_DIRECT on Linux. Its three alignment
requirements: offsets and lengths are whole 4 KiB pages by construction
(records are 12406784 bytes, 3029 pages exactly), but that is a property
of the container in front of us, so it is checked — a misaligned record
makes every read fail EINVAL rather than run slow. Destination buffers
moved from malloc to waste_dio_alloc (posix_memalign). Filesystems may
refuse O_DIRECT anyway, so there is a fallback to plain open plus
posix_fadvise(POSIX_FADV_RANDOM), and when any bank falls back
waste_stats.direct_io goes to 0 and `waste bench` says the hit rate is
partly the kernel's.

vq: rebuild the LUT as an axpy, and put it on the pool — 4.3x

The VQ table build was the wrong shape and single-threaded. For each
8-dim vector it ran `entries` separate eight-element dot products, each
ending in vaddvq_f32 — more time folding four lanes into one than
multiplying — while every other hot path used the thread pool.

Transposing the codebooks to [book][dim][entry] at load (6.5 MB on K3)
turns the build into one axpy per dimension: 32 FMAs produce 16 table
entries with no cross-lane reduction and no wasted lanes. Vectors are
independent, so it also splits across the pool.

Measured on K3:

  decode, 5 steps    LUT build 1.82s -> 0.43s
  prefill, 19 tok    LUT build 7.04s -> 1.64s, total 46.20s -> 41.5s

4.3x on the build, 11% off prefill end to end. Logits move 1.06e-05 —
axpy accumulates in a different order than the dot did — and argmax and
the max logit are unchanged.

accumulated per quantization group so each group's pair of scales
applies once. Weight rows are unpacked to int8 first, which also gave

trunk: leave the embedding table on disk, one row per token

embed_tokens is 1.11 GB of which exactly one row — 7 KB — is read per
token. Keeping it resident bought nothing and cost the expert cache,
which at these budgets is the thing that decides throughput. It now
stays in trunk.bin and the row is pread on use, through the same fd the
loader already opens. Bit-identical logits (max|diff| 0.000e+00).

Resident trunk 28.61 -> 27.50 GB, floor 30.38 -> 29.27 GB at ctx 4096.

waste_tensor grows an on_disk flag with the file offsets, so the
mechanism generalizes; embed_tokens is just the only tensor that
currently qualifies. Everything else in the trunk — the attention
projections, the shared experts, the latent projections — is touched in
full on every token, so streaming it would cost far more I/O than the
freed cache saves.

Honour the RAM budget: stream the trunk, and count the scratch

waste.h calls ram_budget_bytes a hard ceiling. On K3 it was not one.
Peak RSS ran 1.4-3.4 GB over a budget set near the floor, from two
independent causes.

load_trunk slurped trunk.bin whole and then copied every tensor out of
that buffer, so loading needed twice the trunk resident — 57 GB on K3,
before a single token. Nothing wanted the whole file at once; each
tensor knows its own offset, so it now preads them one at a time. Load
also drops from 34s to 20s, most of the difference being the memory
pressure the second copy caused.

waste_plan_memory guessed scratch at a flat 64 MB + hidden*64*4. The
decode buffers alone are 252 MB on K3 (e_gate/e_up/e_down), and the
chunked-prefill buffers — up to ~500 MB at WASTE_CHUNK_MAX, allocated on
first use and never freed — were not counted at all. It now computes
them from the config. K3's floor goes 29.69 -> 30.38 GB, which is the
honest number.

WASTE_CHUNK_MAX moves to model.h

mla: absorb kv_b_proj, cache the latent instead of expanded K and V

The engine was caching K and V expanded per head — 96x192 + 96x128
floats per token per layer, 120 KB — when MLA exists precisely so that
only the 512-wide latent and the 64 rope dims need storing, 2.25 KB.
tools/memplan.py had always computed the latent figure; the C engine
was the half that diverged.

kv_b_proj now moves off the per-cached-token path onto the per-step one:

    q_nope . (W_kb c) == (W_kb^T q_nope) . c
    sum_s a_s (W_vb c_s) == W_vb (sum_s a_s c_s)

so the query is absorbed before scoring and the values are accumulated
in latent space and projected once. Heads stay independent throughout,
so the whole attention — absorption, scores, softmax, output projection
— runs on the pool; the expanded version ran that loop on one core.

Same numbers: max|diff| 1.19e-05 against the expanded path, rel
6.28e-07, argmax and top-5 identical (fp reassociation only).

What it buys, measured on K3:

The recurrence ran on one core while everything else used the pool.
Heads own disjoint K x V slices of the state, so the split is clean and
bit-identical (verified: max|diff| 0.000e+00 against the serial logits).
Splitting at the call site rather than inside kda.c keeps the NEON
dispatch in play.

Measured on K3, 5 decode steps: the kda bucket goes 4.23s -> 3.78s, so
about 2% off the whole step. It is not more because that bucket is the
whole KDA layer, and the layer is dominated by its projections — q, k,
v, o and the full-rank gate are ~440M weights per layer, ~30G MAC per
token across 69 layers, against 868 MFLOP for the recurrence itself.

Note for future profiling: WASTE_THREADS=1 is not a valid serial
baseline on this machine. Only 6 of 18 logical cores are performance
cores, and a single-threaded process gets scheduled onto an E-core —
the same kernel reads 17.21s that way against 4.23s with the pool idle
alongside it.

Q3G trunk: implemented, measured, and not adopted

The trunk sets the RAM floor and the floor decides how much cache is left,
so its bit width is the main lever on hit rate. At 4 bits K3's floor leaves
15.6 GB of cache against a 17 GB per-token working set — just under the
threshold Gate 5 identified — so 3 bits was worth trying.

  trunk   floor      cache    hit    tok/s
  4 bit   40.7 GB   15.6 GB   10%    0.29
  3 bit   34.3 GB   22.0 GB   28%    0.16

The cache prediction held: crossing the working-set threshold nearly
tripled the hit rate. The throughput did not follow — 3 bits is 1.8x
slower, because the entire trunk is unpacked on every token and a 3-bit
bitstream costs much more per weight than 4-bit nibbles (the KDA phase,
mostly trunk matvecs, rises to 32.8% of a token). 4 bits stays the default.

Both widths generate correct code, so 3 bits is not too coarse for the
model — only for the clock. The path is kept and would win if the unpack
were vectorized.

Chunked prefill: 3.3x fewer expert reads, identical logits

waste_model_prefill() runs up to 64 tokens together. The win is not
compute but disk: tokens in a chunk route to overlapping expert sets, so
the distinct-expert count is far below n_tokens * top_k and each is read
once. On a 32-token prompt, against the same prompt one token at a time:

  one at a time   6656 reads  16.53 GB  5.03 s
  chunked         2032 reads   5.05 GB  3.85 s

Logits identical to 6.7e-06 on values of magnitude ~18 — float noise.
Wired into waste_generate and waste_eval, so the CLI gets it for free.

The first design was wrong and is worth recording: expanding each expert
once and running GEMMs, on the theory that it amortizes over the chunk.
Measured, 16 tokens spread over ~1200 distinct experts — under 3 tokens
each — so expanding 7 M weights to serve 3 vectors loses badly to the LUT.
The shipped version keeps decode's LUT arithmetic and reorganizes only the
I/O; gate/up tables depend on the token but not

Port the engine to K3's architecture (weights still downloading)

Implemented from the released reference code, all behind config detection
so the Kimi-Linear path is untouched:

- latent MoE: routed_expert_down_proj -> experts on the 3584-wide latent
  -> optional norm -> up_proj, with shared experts still on the full
  hidden state. LUT sizing and the VQ matvecs follow the latent width.
- SiTU activation: beta*tanh(g/beta)*sigmoid(g) * linear_beta*tanh(u/lb),
  replacing SiLU-and-multiply in both FFN paths.
- full-rank KDA gate (single g_proj) and the bounded decay gate. The
  latter is a different formula, not a clamp: K3 uses
  lower_bound*sigmoid(exp(A_log)*z) where Kimi-Linear used
  -exp(A_log)*softplus(z).
- Attention Residuals: softmax attention over the block-residual history,
  appended every attn_res_block_size layers, plus the rewritten layer loop
  that carries prefix_sum and block_residual.
- nested text_config and the language_model. tensor prefix.

WASTE_E_RAM_BUDGET instead of swapping), waste_plan_memory computed from

of linking a regex engine, rank-ordered pair merging. The converter now
copies tokenizer.model into the container so a container is
self-contained. Verified against Python tiktoken on 12 cases spanning
English, Italian, code, whitespace, digits

Gate 5: real expert cache, and a version API (0.1.0)

src/ecache.{h,c}: bounded expert cache, LFRU with sampled eviction (the
approximation the Gate 2 simulator uses), open addressing index, budget
expressed in bytes and turned into slots. Reads go through pread with
F_NOCACHE: with a 17 GB container on a 64 GB machine the kernel was
caching everything, so any hit rate measured on top of the page cache
would have been fiction. K3's ~816 GB gets no such help.

Measured over 300 batch-1 decode tokens, budget swept:

  cache %    3.0   6.0   12.1   24.2   48.4   96.8
  hit rate  13.2  40.3   61.9   84.8   93.9   94.2
  simulated 29.4  40.6   54.9   71.9   87.4    ~100

Matches the simulation at the K3-relevant 6% and beats it above 12%, so
the 1.5 tok/s projection for K3 on 64 GB stands.

The disagreement at 3% is the useful part: one token touches 208 experts,
so a cache below that keeps nothing alive to the next token — at 1.5% the
hit rate is exactly zero, 2604 evictions in 2704 access

int8 trunk storage: 5.6 GB freed, exact math kept; SDOT measured and boxed

The user asked for int8+SDOT on the expert matmul. Reporting what the
profile actually showed: that loop is a gather (acc += lut[blk + s*256 +
code]) with no multiply, so SDOT does not apply and ARM has no gather
instruction. Cache-blocking it instead (VQ_TILE, swept — 64/128 tie) took
0.18 -> 0.15 s/token.

SDOT does fit the trunk, which was already stored Q8G but was being
expanded to f32 at load. Three modes now:

  f32 weights          0.15 s/tok  9.5 GB  rel 1.6e-06  top-10 identical
  int8 + f32 math      0.13 s/tok  3.9 GB  rel 1.5e-06  top-10 identical
  int8 + SDOT          0.13 s/tok  3.9 GB  rel 1.2e-02  top-10 REORDERED

SDOT delivers 1.9x on the trunk phases (0.30 -> 0.16 s) but the trunk is
~16% of a token, so end-to-end it ties the exact path while costing four
orders of magnitude of accuracy. Default is therefore int8 storage with
f32 arithmetic; WASTE_SDOT=1 opts into the quantized-activation p

Scope: cross-platform engine with dynamically loaded backends

Follows sqlite-vector's dispatch discipline: one global table of function
pointers, filled with a baseline that is always compiled in, then the best
runtime-detected backend overwrites only the slots it implements, with a
force-CPU escape hatch and name introspection.

  AVX/AVX-512 state, aarch64 dotprod/i8mm via sysctlbyname (macOS),

- src/kda.c is now the universal CPU baseline; src/kda_neon.c the NEON
  specialization, registering over it

Fix the reset button doing nothing or looping the start screen when pressed repeatedly (#719)

* Make the reset button reliable from any screen

Pressing reset repeatedly near app start could do nothing, fade the music
with no reset, or bounce the press-start screen back to itself. Three
defects in the old handler:

- It ran from the ImGui widget, racing the menu state machine; a press
  landing mid-fade was re-advanced by the in-flight transition (the
  press-start loop).
- It always wrote gGamestateNext = MAIN_MENU_FROM_QUIT; once the game was
  already in that state a repeat write is swallowed by the != guard in
  main.c, so nothing happened.
- CM_ResetAudio ran unconditionally, so the music faded even when the
  reset was swallowed.

The widget now only sets an atomic request flag; ApplyPendingReset (top of
push_frame, on the game loop) performs the reset. It alternates between
the two identical FROM_QUIT gamestates so every press trips the gamestate
switch, and re-enters the menus

Start actually looking at validating the effects with Opus

I'm back to doing some sanity checking of the guitar pedal using Claude
Opus, and part of that is running the effects on the host for basic
validation.  That showed up a bug in the mix conversion of the reverb,
but also a floating point corner case that doesn't happen on the pedal,
but does happen on x86, just due to undefined behavior.

So those get fixed, and then running various validation tests to see
that the pedal actually does what it should do, showed that most of the
math helpers are not only sufficient, but have precision far past any
noise floor.  That was not unexpected, but it was good validation.

There was one glaring exception: the single-pole filter coefficient
setup was using approximations that work fine at low frequencies, but
gave increasingly bad answers at higher frequencies.  That ended up
being noticeable in the frequency response of the Klonlike effect, for
example.

feat: let x mode build interfaces and drop x_malloc

Three changes that together give x mode a real memory story.

interface_casting gains an is_x flag, mirroring what any_casting already does.
It copied the method table with rti_array_new and boxed the value with
rti_gc_malloc, so any interface construction crashed without a gc. In x mode it
now references both directly. The table holds compile time fn addresses, so
only its lifetime matters, the same aliasing contract x mode already documents
for any and union. This is what makes std/allocator's allocatable interface,
and therefore vec<T>.alloc, usable from .x.

x_malloc is removed. It allocated the backing store of a vec literal in x mode
with a bare malloc that nothing ever freed, and its own error paths called
rti_throw, which needs the coroutine that x mode never starts. A vec literal in
.x is now a compile error pointing at vec<T>.alloc, which takes an explicit
allocator and frees through deinit.

feat: x mode via .x source files

Replaces the abandoned fn/fx keyword plan with a file level mode: a .n file
compiles as usual, a .x file compiles in x mode with no gc, no coroutine and
no runtime initialization. The keyword approach was dropped because it
coloured the call graph virally and forced std to fork; carrying the mode on
the module keeps std untouched and leaves every .n path unchanged.

The whole is_fx lowering path was still present but unreachable, so this only
replaces its trigger. module_t gains is_x from the source extension,
ast_fndef_new copies it onto every fndef, and the existing gates for the
safepoint, the preemption trampoline, the raw allocation and the main_is_fn
entry fork follow from there. The fx name is gone everywhere: TOKEN_FX and its
parser branches are removed, is_fx is is_x, fx_malloc is x_malloc and the
rtype prefix is xfn.

static bool coff_amd64_instruction_matches_action(
        const amd64_asm_inst_t *operation,
        const coff_amd64_unwind_action_t *action) {
    uint8_t first_reg = 0U;
    uint8_t second_reg = 0U;
    uint32_t stack_offset = 0U;
    switch (action->kind) {
        case COFF_AMD64_PLAN_PUSH_NONVOL:
            return strcmp(operation->name, "push") == 0 &&
                   operation->count == 1U &&
                   coff_amd64_register_operand(operation->operands[0],
                                               &first_reg) &&
                   first_reg == action->reg;
        case COFF_AMD64_PLAN_SET_FPREG:
            return strcmp(operation->name, "lea") == 0 &&
                   operation->count == 2U &&
                   coff_amd64_register_operand(operation->operands[0],
                                               &first_reg) &&
                   coff_amd64_rsp_slot_operand(operation->operands[1],
                                               &stack_offset) &&
                   first_reg == action->reg &&
                   stack_offset == action->value;
        case COFF_AMD64_PLAN_ALLOC:
            return strcmp(operation->name, "sub") == 0 &&
                   operation->count == 2U &&
                   coff_amd64_register_operand(operation->operands[0],
                                               &first_reg) &&
                   first_reg == 4U;
        case COFF_AMD64_PLAN_SAVE_NONVOL:
            return strcmp(operation->name, "mov") == 0 &&
                   operation->count == 2U &&
                   coff_amd64_rsp_slot_operand(operation->operands[0],
                                               &stack_offset) &&
                   coff_amd64_register_operand(operation->operands[1],
                                               &second_reg) &&
                   stack_offset == action->value &&
                   second_reg == action->reg;
        case COFF_AMD64_PLAN_SAVE_XMM128:
            return strcmp(operation->name, "movxmm128") == 0 &&
                   operation->count == 2U &&
                   coff_amd64_rsp_slot_operand(operation->operands[0],
                                               &stack_offset) &&
                   coff_amd64_register_operand(operation->operands[1],
                                               &second_reg) &&
                   stack_offset == action->value &&
                   second_reg == action->reg;
        default:
            return false;
    }
}

            0x00U,
            0x00U,
            0x80U,
    };

    assert(ld_elf_dynamic_encode_relocations(
                   relocations,
                   sizeof(relocations) / sizeof(relocations[0]), encoded,
                   sizeof(encoded)) == LD_ELF_DYNAMIC_OK);
    assert(memcmp(encoded, expected, sizeof(expected)) == 0);

    assert(ld_elf_dynamic_encode_relocations(NULL, 0U, NULL, 0U) ==
           LD_ELF_DYNAMIC_OK);
    assert(ld_elf_dynamic_encode_relocations(NULL, 1U, encoded,
                                             LD_ELF64_RELA_SIZE) ==
           LD_ELF_DYNAMIC_INVALID_ARGUMENT);
    assert(ld_elf_dynamic_encode_relocations(relocations, 1U, NULL,
                                             LD_ELF64_RELA_SIZE) ==
           LD_ELF_DYNAMIC_INVALID_ARGUMENT);

    uint8_t before[sizeof(encoded)];
    memset(encoded, 0x5a, sizeof(encoded));
    memcpy(before, encoded, sizeof(encoded));
    assert(ld_elf_dynamic_encode_relocations(
                   relocations,
                   sizeof(relocations) / sizeof(relocations[0]), encoded,
                   sizeof(encoded) - 1U) ==
           LD_ELF_DYNAMIC_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL);
    assert(memcmp(encoded, before, sizeof(encoded)) == 0);
    assert(ld_elf_dynamic_encode_relocations(relocations, 1U, encoded,
                                             LD_ELF64_RELA_SIZE + 1U) ==
           LD_ELF_DYNAMIC_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL);
    assert(memcmp(encoded, before, sizeof(encoded)) == 0);

    const size_t overflowing_count = SIZE_MAX / LD_ELF64_RELA_SIZE + 1U;
    assert(ld_elf_dynamic_encode_relocations(
                   relocations, overflowing_count, NULL, 0U) ==
           LD_ELF_DYNAMIC_OVERFLOW);

fix(test): give build_target outputs a .exe suffix on Windows

config_init only rewrites the default output name "main" to "main.exe", so
the custom names this harness sets ("target_main", ...) stayed extensionless.
The COFF link still succeeded, but Windows cannot execute a PE binary without
the extension, so exec_output() returned nothing and the first assertion
failed with an empty actual value:

  Assert (str_equal(output, expect)) failed: entry 'main.n' output mismatch
  expect: entry:buildtarget.main
  actual:

The harness is in the same position as an explicit -o, which nature honours
verbatim by design (BUILD_OUTPUT_EXPLICIT), so it has to supply the suffix
itself.

Checked the other assertions against Windows semantics while here:
cmd/plat.windows.n returns 'variant' like the darwin/linux variants, so the
cmd expectations are unchanged, and module_source_diag_path normalises
separators to '/' (20260726_01_module_errors already asserts such a path
successfully on Windows).

feat(module): multi-file directory modules

Module identity is now (PackageInstanceId, ModulePath) instead of being
derived from the source file name. A file whose first statement is
`mod <ident>` joins the directory module for its directory; files without
`mod` remain standalone modules exactly as before.

Why: a module could previously only ever be one file, so packages grew
either god-files or artificial `pkg.sub.leaf` import paths. Splitting a
module across files now costs one header line.

Compiler:
- new src/module_index.{c,h} owns the package scan, `mod` validation and
  the module/slot indexes; the scan is deterministic (sorted dir entries,
  slots, sources and units) and stops at a nested package.toml
- module_t holds a slice of source_file_t; top-level declarations are
  shared across parts while imports and aliases stay file-local
- analyzer split into analyzer_module_decls/analyzer_module_bodies so all
  parts' declarations are collected before any function body is analyzed

kv-cache : optimize restoring non-contiguous cells (#27991)

* kv cache : batch state restore scatter reads per contiguous run

When restoring state into non-contiguous destination cells (e.g. a
prompt-cache snapshot into a fragmented ring), state_read_data issued
one small copy per KV cell - ~1.4M copies of a few KiB each for a
40k+ token restore, taking 25-63 s on the CUDA backend.

The snapshot stores cell rows in cell order, so a maximal run of
consecutive destination indices maps to one contiguous block and can
be restored with a single copy. Precompute the runs once and use them
in all three scatter loops (K, V, transposed V). Byte-identical.

The on-device reader copies with a byte cursor when the read and
write chunking differs, so the batched reads are safe for it as well.
Batching makes equal tensor counts with a different split reachable
(save ranges [2,1] vs restore runs [1,2]); the next commit teaches the
reader's 1:1 path to fall back to the byte cursor in that case.

fix: terminate immediately on asar integrity violation (#53433)

* fix: terminate immediately on asar integrity violation

The JS-side asar integrity check ends the process via
process.reallyExit(1), which bottoms out in libc exit(). That runs
atexit handlers and static destructors on the main thread while
Chromium's threads are still live, and on Windows intermittently
dies with an access violation (0xC0000005) before reaching
ExitProcess, so the process exits with the wrong code. Terminate
via base::Process::TerminateCurrentProcessImmediately instead so
nothing else runs and exit code 1 is preserved.

fix: backport Node.js cleanup hook fixes for node::ObjectWrap addons (#53390)

* fix: backport Node.js cleanup hook fixes for node::ObjectWrap addons

Node.js 24.19.0 made node::ObjectWrap register an environment cleanup
hook but did not carry the fix that makes RemoveEnvironmentCleanupHook()
safe to call from ~ObjectWrap() during garbage collection, so any addon
built against the 24.19.0+ headers aborts with
"Assertion failed: (env) != nullptr" once one of its wrapped objects is
collected while no context is entered.

  hooks" (68321eff80918e324e9fdaf1aa8cee6db14b84f7 on nodejs/node main).
* nodejs/node#65630 "src: fix use-after-free in CleanupHookThunkRun" at
  dd2fa31b1d99e5a6710e08ce4139da7c2e344598 and its regression cctest at
  fd325a7fc2b33839c024220aa0c44b9104749686 (not yet landed upstream).

Fixes: https://github.com/electron/electron/issues/53387
